t.abbas abad@36.4,56.4:
Out on the old road from Tehran to Mashhad, somewhere between Shahrud and Sabzevar, the Alborz foothills drift away to the north and the edges of the great salt desert creep up from the south. Abbās Ābād lies on this corridor, a modest settlement known to travellers for its caravanserai, one of the roadside inns built under Safavid rule when Shah Abbas I in the early seventeenth century invested heavily in the pilgrim and trade route to the shrine city of Mashhad. In 2023 dozens of Iran's caravanserais, including ones along this road, were inscribed together as a World Heritage Site.

A caravanserai is a fortress for merchants: a single gate big enough for loaded camels, a courtyard surrounded by vaulted rooms, stables behind, and thick mud brick or fired brick walls to keep out raiders and the desert wind. They were placed roughly a day's journey apart, which on this road means you can still count them off as you ride. Local tradition in the Abbasabad area links some of its people to Georgians resettled by Shah Abbas, part of the mass population moves of his reign; it is a story you may hear over tea.

The riding is honest desert highway. Road 44 is broad, mostly divided or wide two lane, and carries heavy trucks and buses between Tehran and Mashhad around the clock. Surfaces are generally good, but drivers overtake in ways that will keep you alert, and crosswinds across the open plain can be strong. In summer the midday heat is punishing; ride early, rest through the afternoon, and go again in the evening light, when the mountains turn pink and the desert to the south goes silver.

Iran is a big undertaking for a foreign rider. You will need a carnet de passages for your bike, and the rules for foreigners and visas change, so check current conditions before you plan. Fuel is very cheap and available along the main highway, but tourists sometimes have to rely on station attendants' cards, so keep your tank topped up and carry cash. Tea, bread, kebab and dizi, the meat and chickpea stew, are easy to find at roadside restaurants.

There are no towns of any size immediately around Abbās Ābād, so plan your fuel and water between Shahrud to the west and Sabzevar to the east, and treat any caravanserai with a café as a gift.
t.abr@36.8,55.1:
Abr means cloud in Persian, and the name is exact. On the northern slopes of the Alborz mountains, where the humid air from the Caspian Sea rises and condenses, a belt of old forest lies in cloud for much of the year, and anyone riding through it can find themselves in a wet white room with the road vanishing after twenty metres. This is the Hyrcanian forest, a band of broadleaf woodland that stretches along the southern Caspian coast and is up to fifty million years old, a survivor from before the ice ages. UNESCO listed parts of it in 2019, and the forest at Abr, with its beech, oak and hornbeam trees, belongs to the same green belt.

The trees here grow tall and straight, covered in moss and ferns, and in autumn the forest turns rust and gold. The woods shelter wild boar, roe deer, brown bears, and, very rarely, the Persian leopard, which is among the great cats you do not expect to find within a day's drive of a city. The road that crosses the range from the dry Shahroud side to the green Golestan side is one of the finest in northern Iran, a long series of hairpins and long curves climbing to a high pass and dropping through the cloud.

The riding is demanding. Fog and drizzle can come in without warning, the road is narrow in places, and trucks are slow on the climbs and fast on the descents. The surface is generally paved but can be broken by landslides, and the edges are sometimes unprotected. Dress for cold and wet, since temperatures at the top are far below those on the plain, and take the fog seriously. Lights on, speed down.

Āzādshahr is thirty kilometres away and has fuel, bakeries and a bazaar, and Shahroud on the other side of the mountains has more. Do not count on petrol in the forest. Local food includes grilled fish from the Caspian, rice with herbs and walnut sauces, and strong tea. Entry and travel conditions in Iran can be complicated for foreign riders, so check before you plan. A pull-over in the evening, with the cloud drifting among the trees and the smell of wet leaves, is a moment that stays with you.
t.mayamey@36.4,55.7:
Draw a line east from Shahroud along the old road to Khorasan and Mayamey is where the country starts to change its mind. To the north the Alborz mountains lean down, dark with forest on their far side, and to the south the land flattens and dries towards the great central deserts of Iran. Mayamey sits in that seam, in Semnan province, a modest agricultural town with a long history of being passed through.

That history is the point. For centuries this was the way from the capital region towards Nishapur, Mashhad and Central Asia, a branch of what we now loosely call the Silk Road, and the Safavid shahs, Shah Abbas above all, spent real money on caravanserais and bridges so that trade and pilgrims could keep moving. Several of those brick travellers' halls survive across this part of Iran, and the name Abbas Abad on the ride tells you which period of building we are in. They were laid out as a square courtyard with arcaded rooms on all sides, a well in the middle and a gate big enough for loaded camels, and standing in one you can feel exactly how the day ended for a caravan: unload, water the animals, eat, sleep behind a locked door.

For a rider the logic is similar. The roads here are long and open, the kind where you can see a lorry six kilometres away, and the main hazard is not corners but distance and sun. Carry water, wear more sunscreen than you think sensible, and watch for crosswinds where the road crosses open ground. The best months are April, May and October, when the plains are green or golden and not yet anvil-hot. In midsummer the air shimmers and the early start becomes essential.

The villages are tidy mud-brick and concrete places with walnut and pomegranate trees, and nearer the mountains you reach cooler air, orchards and the beginnings of forest. Abr, the forest village on the ride, is the green counterweight to all this dryness, and the contrast is the best reason to ride up there.

I do not know of a particular marked monument at this exact point, so think of Mayamey as a staging post. Shahroud is the larger town for fuel, supplies and a proper meal before or after, and in a place this size you can usually find tea, flatbread, eggs and yoghurt without trouble if you ask.
t.thames@-37.1,175.5:
Thames is the gateway to the Coromandel, and it behaves like one, a handsome, slightly worn gold town that still has a main street of old verandahs and a stack of heritage stories. In the 1860s the strike of gold in the nearby hills brought thousands of diggers, and for a few years this was one of the largest towns in New Zealand. The mines have gone, but the School of Mines building and the mineral museum are reminders, and the long tidal flats on the Firth of Thames in front of the town are a world-class stopover for migrating shorebirds.

For a rider, Thames is the point where you decide what you need before the peninsula swallows you. The town has about seven thousand people, so fuel, groceries, repair shops and cafés are all here, and farther north the supply thins. The climb to Coromandel town runs along State Highway 25, which hugs the western shore of the Firth with the sea only a few metres from your wheels, past bays shaded by pohutukawa trees. The road is narrow and winding, with frequent blind corners, tight turns and the occasional logging truck or camper van, so ease through and use the pull-offs to let faster traffic by. In December the pohutukawa burst into red flowers, and the display is genuinely spectacular.

Inland from the town, the Kauaeranga valley climbs into the Coromandel ranges, where the kauri logging history is on show. Settlers cut the giant kauri trees for ship timbers, and they built huge dams in the valleys to flush logs down in a wall of water, some of which still survive in the forest. Walking tracks lead up from the valley road to old dam sites and views of the whole peninsula.

The weather is changeable, and the range often catches heavy showers while the town stays dry. Summer is busy, with the roads full of holidaymakers, while March and April offer settled weather and quieter roads. Whatever you do, eat a pie in Thames, and have fish and chips on the foreshore as the tide comes in.
t.golestan@37.4,55.8:
Golestan means the land of flowers, and the national park that carries the name is Iran's oldest, set aside in 1957 on the northern slopes of the Alborz mountains. It is a place of sharp contrasts. On one side, the dry steppe of the Turkmen plains, with wheat fields, horses and long horizons, stretches toward the Central Asian border. On the other, the humid forest of the Caspian slopes rises into mist, with ancient oak, hornbeam and beech. In a few hours you can pass from desert scrub to dense green woodland.

The nearest town is Kalaleh, about thirty kilometres away, with some 34,000 people, and it has fuel, shops and simple restaurants. A little farther on, Gonbad-e Qabus is home to a remarkable brick tower, nearly fifty-three metres high, built in 1006 as a tomb for a local ruler, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage site. The region's Turkmen people are famous for their horses, their carpets and their hospitality, and a market day in the small towns is a bright and noisy affair.

The ride through the park climbs a road of tight bends and steep gradients, shaded by trees and often damp. Wildlife is the reward: leopards, brown bears and wild boar live here, though you are unlikely to see them, and the birdlife is rich, with eagles, vultures and woodpeckers. Surfaces vary, and rain can leave mud and fallen branches on the road, so ride with care. Winter brings snow on the heights.

Spring and early summer are the best seasons, when the meadows bloom and the air is mild. In autumn the forest turns red and gold. Carry water and food, since services are few, and fill the tank in Kalaleh or Gonbad before you go. At dusk the forest is full of sound, with birds calling and leaves rustling.
t.northland bay of islands weekend@-36.8,1:
The pin falls on Waiheke Island, a long, hilly island in the Hauraki Gulf, about forty minutes by ferry from downtown Auckland, and it is a very different world from the mainland. The island is a patchwork of vineyards, olive groves, pohutukawa-fringed bays and rolling pasture, with winding roads and sudden views of the blue gulf. About nine thousand people live here, many of them commuters, artists and wine makers, and in summer the island fills with visitors drawn by its beaches, restaurants and cellar doors. Pakuranga, on the Auckland side, is the closest large suburb across the water.

Waiheke has a gentle history. Māori settled the island centuries ago and valued it for its sheltered bays and fertile soil, and European farmers arrived in the nineteenth century, followed by a long period as a quiet holiday island of baches. In the late twentieth century, winemakers found that the warm, dry microclimate and clay soils suited red grapes, especially Bordeaux-style blends, and the island's reputation grew. The main village, Oneroa, has a pretty beach, shops and cafés, and Onetangi, on the north coast, has a long surf beach.

Taking a motorcycle across is a matter of planning. A vehicle ferry runs from the Auckland side, so check timetables and book ahead, since space is limited, especially at weekends. The island roads are narrow, hilly and winding, with gravel patches, blind corners and few barriers, and the speed limit is low. Sheep, cyclists and tourists on hired scooters are all part of the traffic. In wet weather, the clay can be slippery, and the roads are patched.

Fuel is available on the island, though choices are limited, so it is sensible to fill the tank in Auckland before boarding. The northern ride to the Bay of Islands is a long haul, about two hundred kilometres from the city, along State Highway 1 and then smaller roads through Whangārei, so start early. Summer is warm and busy, and winter is mild and quiet, with empty beaches. Take the evening ferry back, with the city's lights spreading across the water, for the best view.
t.northland bay@-36.8,175.1:
The Hauraki Gulf is full of islands, and the pin falls on one of the best known. Waiheke, a short ferry ride east of Auckland, is a hilly island of roughly nine thousand residents, with bays of white sand, wooded gullies and, over the last few decades, a collection of vineyards that makes it the country's most famous wine island. The coordinates fall in its eastern end, a quieter place of farms and coves, and the label that links it to Northland is little more than a convenient finish line.

A weekend in Northland and the Bay of Islands is a long run, with hundreds of kilometres of highway and winding coast, and it usually ends back in the Auckland region rather than on a ferry. If you do finish here, the bike goes on a vehicle ferry from the city, which takes about forty minutes and gives a lovely view of the harbour and the volcanic cones of the Gulf. The roads on Waiheke are narrow and hilly, with tight bends, sheep and cattle grazing beside them, and loose gravel on the verges. Speed limits are low, and the island is best taken slowly, with stops at lookouts over Hauraki Gulf.

The vines grow well on the sunny, dry slopes, and the island is known for red wines made from Cabernet and Merlot blends, and for olive oil. Restaurants at the wineries serve platters of local seafood and cheese, and booking is wise in summer. The island also has a thriving community of artists and craftspeople, with studios open to visitors. Beaches such as Onetangi, a long sweep of sand, and Oneroa, closer to the ferry, are popular.

Fuel is limited, with a couple of stations in the main villages, so fill up in Auckland if you can, and check ferry times and fares, since the island fills up in summer. Pakuranga and Manukau on the mainland have all services. Weather is mild, but wind and showers can arrive fast, so bring a light waterproof.
t.coromandel town@-36.8,175.5:
Coromandel Town is the real thing: a small, unhurried settlement of around fifteen hundred people on the west side of the peninsula, facing the Hauraki Gulf at the head of a quiet harbour. It is the last proper town before the road goes feral in the north, and it earns its place on the Auckland loop as a lunch stop and a point of arrival, since the road in from Thames is one of the great coastal rides in the country.

That road, State Highway 25, is the hero. It clings to the shore of the Firth of Thames for nearly fifty kilometres, with big pōhutukawa trees arching overhead and the tide often only a metre below the verge. In December the trees flower scarlet. It is slow, narrow and bendy enough that the average speed is low, so give it time and watch for campervans coming the other way, wide on the hairpins. After the shore the road climbs and drops over the ridge at the Coromandel Range, which has its own tight corners, then rolls down to the town.

Gold made this town. The 1860s rush brought thousands of prospectors, and the harbour was busy with ships. After the gold gave out, the timber industry, with its kauri forests, and later farming and tourism kept the town going. Some old buildings along the main street retain their wooden verandas, and a small mining museum tells the story. The Driving Creek Railway, built by a potter, climbs through native bush and is one of the more unusual attractions of the area.

For the rider, the town is simple and easy. There is a petrol station, a bakery, a few cafes and a pub or two, and you can fill up and eat without fuss. Whitianga, on the east side and about twenty kilometres away, is bigger and has more choice for both. The famous smoked mussels and the fresh seafood are the dish to choose here.

Plan the timing: summer holidays bring crowds, and the roads fill with rental vans and trailers. Autumn is quieter, with warm days and still seas. Winter brings rain and cold, but also solitude, and a rider with decent waterproofs has the peninsula nearly to himself.
t.waiouru@-39.5,175.7:
Waiouru is a military town on the edge of a desert, which sounds like a joke but is simply geography. The settlement sits at about 800 metres on the central plateau of the North Island, in the rain shadow of the three great volcanoes, and the surrounding land of tussock, gravel and wind-bent scrub gets the name Rangipo Desert because of its dry, stony look. In truth it receives plenty of rain, but the soil drains instantly and little grows.

Around thirteen hundred people live here, many connected to the army base, and the National Army Museum, which tells the story of the New Zealand army from the colonial wars to modern peacekeeping, is the main attraction. It is a thoughtful and well-presented museum, with uniforms, vehicles and personal letters, and it is worth an hour if the weather is bad, which it often is. Waiouru is the highest settlement on the main highway, and snow and ice can close State Highway 1 for hours in winter.

The Desert Road, which runs north from here to Turangi, climbs to about 1,074 metres, the highest point on the New Zealand state highway network. It crosses a bleak and beautiful plain, with Ruapehu, Ngauruhoe and Tongariro filling the western horizon, and the long straights and sweeping rises suit a relaxed pace. Wind is the great enemy, since it can hit with surprising force, and snow, ice and fog are all possible in any month except mid-summer. Check the road report before setting out, because the road is closed several times each winter.

Beside the road, a memorial recalls the Tangiwai disaster of Christmas Eve 1953, when a lahar from Ruapehu's crater lake swept away a railway bridge just before the Auckland express arrived, killing 151 people. It is a sombre reminder that the mountains are alive, and Ruapehu erupted again in the mid-1990s.

Fuel is available in Waiouru, which is important because the next services are a long way along the road, and the cold can drain a tank quickly. Cafes and bakeries serve hot pies and strong coffee, a well-worn tradition among travellers heading through. Fill up, dress warmly and go.

Aim for a clear morning, when the volcanoes stand out, and the long road ahead feels like an invitation.
t.turangi@-39.0,175.8:
Turangi is a fishing town that was built almost overnight. In the 1960s, when the Tongariro Power Scheme needed workers to divert the rivers of the central plateau into hydroelectric stations, a new town was laid out beside the Tongariro River at the southern end of Lake Taupō. About three and a half thousand people live there now, and the place has settled into an easy life based on trout, tourism and the great volcanic national park behind it.

The trout come first. The Tongariro River is one of the most famous trout rivers in the world, with rainbow trout swimming up from the lake to spawn in winter, and fishermen stand shoulder to shoulder in the pools in waders, casting long lines. The town calls itself the trout fishing capital of the world, and the claim is only half a joke. Nearby, the Tokaanu thermal pools offer hot springs fed by volcanic heat, and the walk through the geothermal area has bubbling mud and steaming vents.

Turangi is also the base for the Tongariro Alpine Crossing, a walk across a volcanic landscape of craters, coloured lakes and lava flows that is often called the best day walk in the country. The crossing is strenuous, and the weather on the volcanoes can turn deadly cold, so many people take shuttles from town before dawn. Ngauruhoe, the cone that stood in for Mount Doom in the films, rises beside it.

For riders, the town is the end of the Desert Road, with a long descent from the plateau to the lake. State Highway 1 continues along the western edge of the lake to Taupō, with bends and views of the water. Frost and fog can be present on winter mornings, and heavy traffic builds up on holiday weekends. The surface is good and the gradients gentle, and the lake is always on one side.

Fuel is easy here, with stations on the main road, and shops and cafes in the centre. The lakeside is a good place for a break, with picnic tables and a view of the mountains across the water.

Come in autumn if you can, when the light is clear, the crowds have gone and the trout run is beginning. The water in the lake is blue, and the volcanoes look close enough to touch.
t.whitianga@-36.8,175.7:
Whitianga lies on the east side of the Coromandel Peninsula, on the shore of Mercury Bay, a wide, sheltered, sandy bay that has been popular with sea-goers for almost a thousand years. The Māori navigator Kupe is said to have landed here, and in 1769 Captain Cook anchored in the bay to observe the transit of Mercury, giving the bay its English name. Today it is a relaxed little resort town of three or four thousand people, built around a marina, a long beach and a long tradition of fishing, and it is the best base on this side of the Coromandel.

Getting here is half the pleasure. From the west the road crosses the spine of the peninsula, a steep, winding switchback through dense native bush and tree ferns, the kind of surface that rewards patience and punishes impatience. On the east side it opens into farmland and coast, and the sea appears suddenly in a flash of blue. The roads are narrow, often damp, and frequently shaded, so look for gravel and slippery leaf litter in the corners, and expect a lot of caravans and campervans in summer. Between Christmas and the end of January, when the pohutukawa trees are in crimson flower along the shore, the whole coast looks as if it has been painted.

In town, a small passenger ferry runs across the harbour to Ferry Landing, a few minutes away, and from there tracks and boat trips lead to the area's best-known spots. Cathedral Cove, a huge arched cave carved by the waves, and Hot Water Beach, where you can dig your own thermal pool in the sand at low tide, both lie within easy distance, and both get crowded in high season. Go early or late and they are much better.

Whitianga has fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and plenty of cafes, and the local seafood is excellent, especially the scallops and the fresh fish. For anywhere larger you must head back toward Thames, which is a good hour or more away. In winter the days are short and the roads damp, but the town is quiet and the coast has a moody, windswept charm of its own.
t.rotorua@-38.1,176.3:
Rotorua announces itself with a smell. The sulphur drifting from the geothermal fields has an eggy tang that takes a few minutes to get used to, and then you stop noticing. The town of about sixty-five thousand people sits on the shore of Lake Rotorua, inside an ancient volcanic caldera, and the ground beneath it steams, bubbles and spurts in a way that makes the place unlike anywhere else in the country.

The Te Arawa people have lived here for centuries, using the hot pools for cooking and bathing, and the cultural heart of the area is at Whakarewarewa, where a living village still cooks in steaming ground and bathes in natural pools. The Pōhutu geyser, nearby, can shoot water up to thirty metres into the air, several times a day. Hāngī, a feast cooked in an earth oven, is the local food to try, and it is not difficult to find. The Government Gardens, with a handsome Tudor-style bathhouse built in 1908, tell the other side of the story, when the town was a spa for Edwardian visitors.

The nearby forest is a surprise. Whakarewarewa Forest, planted in the early twentieth century, includes giant Californian redwoods, with a canopy walk and mountain bike trails running through their shade. The lake holds Mokoia Island, the setting of the romantic legend of Hinemoa, who swam across the water to meet her lover Tūtānekai, guided by the sound of his flute. The lakes around the town are blue, green or milky depending on minerals.

For a rider, Rotorua is a good base. The roads south towards Taupō and the national park are smooth, with long bends through forest and farmland, and are best on a dry morning. Traffic is heavy at times, with trucks hauling logs, and fog can sit in the valleys at dawn. The rain can be heavy, and the ground can steam in the cold.

Fuel and services are abundant, with stations and workshops all over town, and Tokoroa, about thirty-five kilometres south, is another large centre. Eat something local, then go.

Leave early, with the smell of sulphur behind you, and head south towards the volcanoes. The day will be long, and it will be full.
t.second component@-39.0,175.7:
Tongariro National Park holds three volcanoes, two of them regularly in the headlines, and the coordinates here fall at the northern edge of the park, a few kilometres from Turangi. The park was the first in New Zealand, created in 1887, when the paramount chief Te Heuheu Tūkino IV gifted the sacred summits to the Crown, in order to protect them from being carved up and sold. It is also a dual World Heritage Site, listed for both its natural and its cultural value, a rare distinction.

The three peaks are Tongariro, Ngāuruhoe and Ruapehu, and they could hardly be more different. Ngāuruhoe is the near-perfect cone, young and steep, with a scree-covered flank that gives it a sinister look. Tongariro is a complex of craters, lava flows and bright lakes, including the Emerald Lakes, coloured by dissolved minerals. Ruapehu, the highest, at about 2,800 metres, carries a crater lake and the largest ski fields in the North Island. All three are active, and the eruptions of Tongariro in 2012 and Ruapehu in the 1990s remind visitors that the landscape is alive.

The country around Tokaanu, close to this point, is full of steam. The thermal area has hot springs, mud pools and a small walk along a boardwalk, and the pools are a good way to warm up after the cold air of the plateau. The lake, Taupō, lies to the north, vast and blue, and the winds that blow across it can be strong and sudden.

Riding here is open and scenic, with State Highways 1 and 47 offering long bends and views of the volcanoes. In winter, snow and ice can appear on the roads, and the weather can turn within minutes. Fog and rain are common on the western side, and wind can be fierce. The traffic is generally light, though busy on summer weekends and during ski season.

Fuel is available in Turangi, only about seven kilometres away, with stations, supermarkets and cafes. It is the sensible place to fill up and eat before going into the park.

Look for the early morning light, when the volcanoes are sharp against the sky. It is a landscape that deserves a slow approach.
t.first component@-39.3,175.6:
Whakapapa is where Tongariro National Park lives most of the time. The coordinates fall on the north-western side of the park, near the village at the foot of Mount Ruapehu, a cluster of lodges, a visitor centre and the stately Chateau Tongariro, a grand hotel that opened in 1929 and still stands against the mountain like something from an Alpine postcard. In winter the village is a ski resort, and in summer it is a trailhead for walkers.

Ruapehu is the largest active volcano in New Zealand, rising to about 2,800 metres, with a crater lake that sits at its summit. It erupted violently in 1995 and 1996, scattering ash across the plateau and closing the ski fields, and there is a constant watch on the lake temperature. Some of the old lahar channels are still visible on the slopes. A chairlift runs up the mountain in both summer and winter, giving an easy way to see the upper landscape.

The riding is very good. State Highway 48 climbs gently from the plateau road through beech forest, with gentle bends and views of the mountain, and finishes at the village. The road is short but pleasant, and in clear weather the view of the peak is superb. Be careful in winter, when ice and snow can make the climb hazardous, and chains may be necessary. Wind is often strong, and cloud can come down suddenly, leaving you in cold mist.

The nearest towns are far enough away to matter. Waiouru, about twenty-four kilometres from this point, and Turangi, about thirty-eight, have fuel, and the village at the mountain does not offer reliable supplies for motorcycles, so fill up before you climb. Cafes in the village serve hot food and drinks, and they are welcome after a cold ride.

Spend an hour walking on one of the short tracks near the village, through beech forest and alpine scrub, to the Taranaki Falls, where a stream plunges over an old lava flow. The smell of the forest, damp and earthy, is memorable.

The best time is in the early morning of a clear day, when the mountain stands clear of the cloud. Late summer and early autumn have the steadiest weather.
t.rotorua@-38.1,176.2:
Rotorua smells of eggs, and everyone is soon used to it. The city sits in the crater of an ancient volcano, on the shore of a lake, and the ground beneath it is alive: steam rises from roadside drains, mud pools bubble in parks, and in the thermal reserve of Te Puia the Pohutu geyser erupts many times a day, throwing a column of boiling water twenty metres or more into the air. The sulphur is the price of living on a hot spot, and the nickname of Rotovegas, half affection and half mockery, covers the tourist bustle.

The land belongs to the Te Arawa, who have lived around the lakes for centuries and who still run living villages. At Whakarewarewa, residents cook food in natural steam boxes and bathe in hot pools, a way of life that continues. A hāngī, a feast cooked in an earth oven heated by hot stones, is one of the best meals to try here. Another chapter of the story lies at Lake Tarawera, where an eruption in 1886 killed many people and buried the famous Pink and White Terraces, once called the eighth wonder of the world. The Buried Village excavates houses covered by ash.

The riding is wonderful. The highways through the central North Island, including the route known as the Thermal Explorer Highway, run through pine forest and farmland, past steaming vents and blue lakes. East of the city, the road toward Lake Waikaremoana, deep in the Te Urewera forest, is a winding, remote route through native bush, with sections that may be unsealed or affected by slips, so check conditions before setting out and carry what you need. Mist and rain can come quickly, and the central plateau can be cold even in summer.

Fuel is easy in Rotorua, a town of more than sixty thousand, with stations on all main roads. The forests of giant redwoods on the edge of town are lovely for a walk after the ride, with trees planted in the early twentieth century. The best months are November to April, and winter mornings can bring frost on the higher roads.
t.le morne@-20.5,57.3:
Le Morne is the dramatic southwest corner of Mauritius, a basalt monolith rising 556 metres from the sea at the end of a narrow peninsula. The mountain has a heavy history: in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, escaped slaves, known as maroons, hid in the caves and on the summit plateau, and according to tradition, when soldiers came to tell them that slavery had been abolished in 1835, they misunderstood and jumped from the cliffs. Whether or not the story is exact, the mountain became a symbol of resistance and freedom, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Small villages lie nearby, such as Petite Case Noyale and Grande Rivière Noire.

The landscape around the mountain is a mix of lagoon and beach on one side, with kitesurfers drawn to the strong winds and flat water, and sugar cane and scrub on the other. The lagoon is a pale turquoise, protected by a reef that you can see as a line of white surf offshore. The roads along the southern coast are narrow and often busy with local traffic, but surfaces are mostly good. Driving is on the left, and local drivers are brisk, with plenty of overtaking.

From Le Morne, the route turns inland toward the Black River Gorges National Park, climbing into the forested highlands. The change is noticeable: the air cools, the vegetation becomes dense, and the road narrows and bends through tropical forest with views toward the coast. The park protects some of the last remnants of native forest on the island, and rare birds such as the pink pigeon and the Mauritius kestrel, which were brought back from the brink of extinction.

For practical needs, fuel is available in the larger villages along the coast, but not on the mountain itself, so fill up before heading to the peninsula. There are small cafes and snack stands selling dholl puri, a thin pancake filled with split peas, and gateaux piments, fried chilli cakes. The best time to visit is the drier, cooler months from May to December. Cyclones are possible from January to March, and rain can be heavy.
t.chamarel@-20.4,57.4:
Chamarel is a farming village folded into the hills of south-west Mauritius, and getting there is half the fun. The road climbs from the coast near Case Noyale through sugar cane and then bends upward in tight, short hairpins, with the tarmac sometimes uneven and the verges thick with palms, vanilla and flowering trees. The air gets cooler and wetter as you rise, and you will smell wet earth and woodsmoke before you see the village. It is a gentle, rolling kind of riding, with surprises, with a local bus or a pickup always round the next bend.

The reason people come is the Seven Coloured Earths, a patch of dunes in reds, browns, violets and greens that formed from the weathering of volcanic rock. The colours settle in layers and, as the guides like to say, do not mix even in the rain. A short way off, the Chamarel waterfall drops about a hundred metres into the forest, and you see it from a platform. The site charges an entrance fee, and there are giant tortoises from Aldabra wandering about in an enclosure, which is a good reason on its own to stop. The coffee grown in the surrounding hills has a following, and the village also has a rum distillery that opens to visitors, in case you need a story to tell your friends about the afternoon you tasted rum on a motorbike. Do the tasting after you ride, not before.

The island's history is written in these hills. Maroon communities, escaped slaves, used the mountains of the south-west as refuges during the French and British colonial periods, and Le Morne, the great rock on the coast, is a monument to them. The forest you ride through now was once a wall behind which people disappeared.

For fuel, do not assume anything on the plateau. The pumps are down at the coast and along the main roads, at places like Chemin Grenier and Case Noyale, so fill up before the climb. Rain showers move through any time of day, even in the dry season, and the polished tarmac on the bends gets slippery. Aim to arrive before the tour buses, which usually reach the earths late morning.
t.black river gorges viewpoint@-20.4,57.4:
The Black River Gorges are the green heart of Mauritius, a national park of upland forest, rivers and waterfalls that covers a large block of the south-west. The viewpoint on the road along the edge of the plateau gives you the best sense of it, because from here the land drops away in a long wooded slope all the way to the Indian Ocean, and on a clear morning you can pick out the sea on the horizon and the pale line of surf around the reef. When clouds sit low on the plateau, which they often do, the view disappears, and the ride turns into a wet, atmospheric tunnel of trees and mist.

This is a good place to think about how fragile the island is. When the Dutch and then the French settled Mauritius, they cleared enormous areas for cane and brought in deer, pigs and macaque monkeys, and the native forest shrank to a few remnants. A good deal of what remains is here. Conservationists have spent decades pulling a few endemic birds back from the brink, the Mauritius kestrel, the pink pigeon and the echo parakeet among them, and the gorges are one of the places you have the chance of seeing them. You are more likely to see monkeys by the road, and it is sensible not to feed them.

The road across the plateau is a quiet, winding one, climbing through tea and forest and bordered by tall, damp tree ferns. The surface is generally fine but the weather can turn it greasy, and in places there are potholes that arrive without warning. Traffic is thin on weekdays and heavier on Sundays, when families head for the lakes and picnics. The temperature can be ten degrees cooler than the coast, so bring a jacket you will be glad of.

Fuel and food are in the lowland towns, Chemin Grenier being the closest large one, so top up before you start across. There are small stalls and a few modest restaurants near the viewpoints, but do not count on them being open. Carry water, wear rain gear, and give yourself time to walk to one of the lookouts, because the sound of the forest is a part of the place.
t.grand bassin@-20.4,57.5:
Grand Bassin sits in the crater of an extinct volcano, high on the central plateau of Mauritius, and it is the holiest place on the island for Hindus. The lake has a quiet, dark look, and around it stand temples, shrines and, towering above the shore, a huge statue of Shiva that was put up in the 2000s. Close by is another statue of the goddess Durga. The place is also called Ganga Talao, and the story goes that in the early 1970s a priest dreamed that the lake was linked with the sacred Ganges, and water carried from India was poured into it. Since then pilgrims have come in numbers, above all at Maha Shivaratri in February or March, when many walk from all over the island in white, carrying decorated wooden frames on their shoulders.

For a rider, the road up from the lowlands is a pleasure. The tarmac twists through sugar cane, then through forest and small villages, with the air getting cooler as you gain height. Nothing is steep for long, but the bends are many and the surface changes from smooth to patched. The area around the lake gets busy at weekends and during festivals, when the road fills with pilgrims on foot, and the parking by the temple can be tight for a motorcycle. Be patient and careful around the walkers.

Dress as you would for a temple: shoulders and knees covered if you go in, shoes off at the temple doors. Visitors are welcome, and the atmosphere is calm, scented with incense and flowers, and punctuated by the cries of the macaques that have claimed the place as theirs. Do not carry food in the open, and do not carry anything you do not want stolen from your hand. The monkeys are quick and fearless.

Grand Bois, five kilometres away, and Chemin Grenier, a bit farther, have pumps and shops. The surrounding hills are part of the Black River Gorges area, and the damp forest is home to endemic plants and a few rare birds. Come in the morning, when the mist hangs on the water and the light is soft, and you will understand why people walk for a day to reach it.
t.curepipe@-20.3,57.5:
Curepipe is the highest of the big towns on Mauritius, at about 550 metres on the central plateau, and it has a climate to match. It is cooler and wetter than the coast, often misty, with drizzle that locals take for granted, and the town has a slightly faded, colonial air, with old wooden houses, verandas and tall trees. The name possibly comes from soldiers cleaning their pipes here on the march. Curepipe has about eighty-four thousand people and runs into Vacoas and Midlands, so services are plentiful, and the end of the Black River Gorges route is a comfortable finish.

The town is known for its crater lake, Trou aux Cerfs, an extinct volcano whose rim offers a wide view over the plateau and the sea on a clear day. It is also the home of the Mauritius Glass Gallery and a famous model ship factory, where intricate replicas of historic vessels are built by hand. The Botanical Garden at Pamplemousses is elsewhere on the island, but near here you can visit Grand Bassin, a sacred crater lake for Hindus, where pilgrims gather for Maha Shivaratri. A huge statue of Shiva stands nearby.

The road in from the gorges passes through tea plantations and forests of cryptomeria, and the heights above are some of the greenest in the country. Corners are frequent, the surface is mostly good with some patches, and rain makes the road slick. Fog can reduce visibility sharply, so lights on and cautious speeds are wise. Traffic builds quickly at the approach to the town, especially at rush hour, when buses, vans and cars fill every lane.

In Curepipe, you can find fuel, banks and restaurants with Creole, Indian and Chinese food, which reflect the island's mix of cultures. Try the local street snacks, like fried noodles and samosas, and drink the sweet vanilla tea from the island. The best time to visit is the dry season, from May to November, when skies are clearer, but even then, you should expect a shower. A hot drink on a damp afternoon is the correct way to finish.
t.revda@56.8,59.9:
Revda is a small Ural industrial town on a river that bears its name, with a reputation that is better than the one its neighbours have. It sits about fifty kilometres west of Yekaterinburg, and its story is that of many Ural towns: in the 1730s, an ironworks was built on the Revda, with a dam and a pond, and a settlement of workers grew around it. Later, copper smelting became the main business, and the Sredneuralsk copper smelter, which operated for most of the Soviet period, left a heavy mark on the surrounding landscape, with bare hills and damaged forest. In recent years, the situation has improved, and the woods are slowly returning.

The town has about sixty thousand residents, in a mix of Soviet blocks and older wooden houses, around the pond at the centre. Pervouralsk, the larger neighbour just to the east, claims a famous monument: an obelisk on the boundary between Europe and Asia, on the old Siberian road, which draws travellers to stand with one foot on each continent. It is a few kilometres from here, and worth a photo stop. The Urals are a very old range, worn down to low, forested hills, so the border is a gentle one, and you cross it without noticing.

For a rider, the roads around Revda are pleasant rather than thrilling. They roll through spruce and birch forest, past ponds and old ironworks villages, and the traffic is moderate, with commuters from Yekaterinburg and the odd heavy lorry. The surface is generally fair, but can have frost damage, and the corners are gentle and open. On weekends in summer, city dwellers head for the lakes and forests, so aim for weekdays or early starts. Weather can be changeable, with sudden storms in July, and the autumn forest is golden.

Fuel and food are easy. The town has petrol stations on its main roads, and supermarkets, cafés and basic hotels, and for anything more complicated, Pervouralsk and Yekaterinburg are close. A café by the pond serves a decent soup, and in summer you can sit outside and watch the anglers.

If you are heading west, this is a good place to top up the tank and the stomach. The Urals ahead are wilder, and services are sparser.
t.satka@55.0,59.0:
White rock is the first thing you notice around Satka. The town sits on the Ai River in the Southern Urals, and the hills nearby are quarried for magnesite, a pale mineral used to make heat-resistant bricks for furnaces and steelworks, so the slopes above the roofs look as though someone has been at them with a knife and a bucket of whitewash. The Satka magnesite works, one of the biggest of its kind in Russia, have been the town's main employer for generations, and the dust and the pits are part of the landscape.

The place began as an ironworks in the 1750s, founded on the river by merchants who recognised the value of the local ore and forest, and for a century the Satka furnaces made iron in the old Ural way, with a dam, a pond and a village of wooden houses. A good deal of that character survives in the older streets, though most of the housing is Soviet. About fifty thousand people live here, and there is a local museum with a decent collection about the region's industry, minerals and the Bashkir people who lived here before the ironworkers came.

The surrounding hills are the real draw for riders. This is the Western flank of the Southern Urals, a region of rounded ridges, spruce and fir forest and clear, cold rivers, and the roads that thread through it have a pleasing, unhurried rhythm: long gentle climbs, forested saddles, and sudden views over wooded valleys. The main road from Chelyabinsk passes nearby, with moderate traffic, and the surface is generally fair, though frost damage is common, and some side roads are gravel. Rain can arrive suddenly, and in the high ground the fog is thick. Summer is short, so the best months are June to September, and autumn colour in the birch and aspen is glorious.

Satka is a good place to restock, since it has several petrol stations, supermarkets and cafés, and a hotel or two. Beyond it, to the south and west, villages are small and services thin, so fill up here. Bakal, about eighteen kilometres off, is another old mining town, built on siderite iron ore, with a faded Soviet feel.

Further up the road lies the national park around Lake Zyuratkul, and the mountains get taller and wilder. If the weather is kind, take the road in the evening, when the ridges glow.
t.kungur@57.4,56.9:
Kungur is a town of merchants that happens to sit on top of a cave. The city has been here since 1648, on a bluff above the Sylva River where it meets the Iren, and in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, it grew rich on trade, especially tea and leather, with a well-built centre of stone shops, warehouses and churches that survives surprisingly well. The old merchant houses on the main streets are low and solid, with fine brickwork and carved details, and the town has a pleasantly faded feel, with a small museum and a cluster of cafés.

The cave is the main attraction. The Kungur Ice Cave, hollowed out of gypsum and anhydrite on the bank of the Sylva, is one of the largest karst caves in Russia, with more than five kilometres of mapped passages and about a kilometre and a half open to visitors. Inside, the galleries are hung with ice crystals, frozen stalagmites and sparkling curtains, and underground lakes lie still and dark. The ice forms in winter and melts partly in summer, and the guides lead groups through the main grottoes with lights and a good deal of storytelling, including legends that Yermak, the Cossack conqueror of Siberia, once passed this way. The temperature inside hovers around freezing, so wear warm clothes even in July. Tours run all year, and the winter visit, when the ice is at its best, is the most magical.

Geologists have another reason to remember Kungur. The Kungurian stage of the Permian period, about two hundred and eighty million years old, takes its name from the town, and the rocks of the region record a time of salt basins and reef.

The riding here is pleasant, especially west of the Urals. The roads run through rolling farmland, spruce forest and river valleys, with gentle bends and long views. The surface is mostly good on the main road from Perm, with some frost damage and patches, and traffic is moderate, with trucks. In summer, the weather is warm and sometimes stormy. September is golden, and winter is cold and snowy.

The town is large enough that you will find petrol stations, shops, cafés and hotels with little trouble, and the cave has a car park and a small cafe. Book ahead for summer weekends, when coaches arrive from Perm. Walk across the old bridge in the evening. The river is wide, and the sun sets behind the cliffs.
t.chusovoy@58.3,57.8:
The Chusovaya is one of the few rivers that cuts straight across the Urals, flowing from east to west through the mountains rather than around them, and Chusovoy is the town where it leaves the hills. The river is famous for its cliffs, called boytsy, or fighters, by locals, tall, grey, sometimes vertical walls of limestone and sandstone that rise directly from the water, and in spring, when the snowmelt turns the river fast and high, rafters come from across Russia to run it. In legend, the Cossack leader Yermak began his march into Siberia in 1581 along this river, with a band of men hired by the wealthy Stroganov family, and the memory of that expedition is part of local pride.

The town grew around an ironworks, founded in the nineteenth century, and later became a centre of metallurgy. About fifty thousand people live here, in an industrial landscape of mills and chimneys along the river, but the surroundings are wooded hills, with spruce and pine on the slopes, and the contrast is striking. A local museum tells something of the history, though I would check opening hours before planning on it.

The riding is good here. The road from Perm runs east through gentle hills, and past Chusovoy, it follows the river valley with views of cliffs and forest, and the bends become more frequent. The surface is generally fair on the main road, though frost damage and patches are common, and lorries slow the pace. In summer, the weather is warm and humid, with thunderstorms in the afternoon, and in autumn, the forest turns red and gold. Spring floods can cover riverside roads, and winter is long and snowy. For a rider, May to September is the sensible window.

Chusovoy is a convenient place to stop, with several petrol stations, a handful of cafés and hotels, and supermarkets, and it is the last sizeable town before the road heads into the mountains. Lyamino, a village just a few kilometres away, is smaller, with basic shops, so fill up in town. If you plan to raft the river, there are local operators in season.

Go down to the water and look at the cliffs. They are ancient, and the river has been cutting through them for a very long time.
t.gubakha@58.8,57.6:
Gubakha is a coal town on the western slope of the Urals, and it makes no apology for it. The Kizel coal basin, a strip of black seams along the foothills of the range, was one of the main coal sources of the Urals from the nineteenth century, and the mines around Gubakha fed the ironworks and railways of the region for generations. Most of the pits have closed in recent years, as the seams ran low and the economics collapsed, and the town has struggled to find a new purpose. About twenty-six thousand people live here, in a tidy grid of Soviet apartment blocks and wooden houses, on the banks of the Kosva River.

The setting is better than the town. The Kosva runs through a wide valley, with forested ridges on either side and, in the distance, the low blue outline of the Kvarkush, a hill range that stretches north. The river is clean and quick, with gravel bars and reed beds, and in spring, it floods across the meadows. The land is spruce, fir and birch, with wild raspberries on the clearings, and the smell of wood smoke in autumn. The old mine spoil heaps, grassy now, give a strange, rolling shape to the horizon.

There has been some effort to turn the area into a sporting centre. A ski resort in the hills near the town draws people from Perm in winter, and the river is popular with canoeists in summer, though I would not promise anything about current facilities. Nearby villages preserve old ways, with wooden houses and gardens.

The ride here from Perm or Chusovoy runs through gentle country, with long, quiet stretches and few vehicles. The road is generally decent, though patched, with the occasional lorry carrying timber or coal. Surfaces degrade on the side roads, where gravel and potholes are common. Expect fog and rain in any month, and be ready for snow from October. The best season is June to September, and September, with the leaves turning, is lovely.

Fuel is not a problem in town, which has several stations, and the shops and cafés cover the basics. A hot meal of soup, pelmeni and tea is easy to find. Ugleuralsky, about twelve kilometres away, is another small mining town, and the roads between them have an end-of-the-line feel. Stop at the river for a few minutes. It is cool, clear, and flowing quietly past the hills.
t.usva@58.7,57.6:
Usva is the name of a small river and a village, and for anyone who has seen photographs of Russia's most dramatic rafting trips, it also means the Usvinskiye Stolby, the Usva Pillars. These are great cliffs of limestone, rising up to a hundred metres from the water, standing along the river in jagged, grey, sometimes overhanging ranks, with caves in the base and pine trees clinging to the ledges. They are among the best known river landscapes in the Urals, and the rafting season in spring, when meltwater makes the Usva fast and cold, brings crowds of paddlers from across the region.

The river runs west from the mountains through a narrow valley, passing woods and meadows, and in places the cliffs close in so tightly that there is barely room for the water. The rock is Permian limestone, riddled with small caves and cracks, and in some places, there are overhangs that look ready to fall. Birds nest in the cliffs, including falcons, and in summer the surrounding forest is full of bird song. In autumn, the leaves turn gold and red, and the cliffs look even more dramatic.

The village is small, a handful of wooden houses and a few shops, in a lonely valley of the Perm region. Gubakha, about eighteen kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, and Shumikhinsky, a few kilometres off, a small settlement with basic services. Do not expect much in the way of tourist infrastructure, though a few guest houses and camps operate in the rafting season, and local people are usually friendly and helpful.

Reaching it is part of the experience. The roads from Perm and Chusovoy run through quiet forest and farmland, with long, gentle sections and the occasional rough patch. Close to the river, the road can be gravel or dirt, and conditions change fast after rain, so a dual-sport bike is better than a heavy tourer. Watch for logging trucks, and for mud. Expect cool nights, even in summer, and be ready for rain at any time. May and June bring high water and the rafting crowds, while July and August are quieter.

Fuel is the main thing to plan. There is none in the village, so fill up in Gubakha before you go. Carry water, snacks, a basic repair kit, and a map. Spend a while looking at the cliffs from the bank. The scale is easy to underestimate until you see a raft beneath them.
t.gonbad e qabus@37.3,55.2:
A single brick tower, a thousand years old, rises out of a park in the middle of a busy town on the edge of the Turkmen steppe, and it is taller than anything around it. Gonbad-e Qabus was built in 1006 or 1007 for Qabus ibn Voshmgir, a ruler of the Ziyarid dynasty and a poet and scholar of some renown, as his tomb. It stands about fifty metres high on an artificial mound, a ten pointed star in plan, topped by a conical roof, built of fired brick with almost no decoration beyond two bands of Kufic inscription. Legend says Qabus's body was hung in a glass coffin from the roof. It became a World Heritage Site in 2012, and it is considered one of the masterpieces of early Islamic architecture, a model for tomb towers across Iran and Central Asia.

The town of Gonbad-e Kavus, named after the tower, is the centre of a region where Turkmen culture is strong, with markets selling carpets, felts and horses; the Turkmen horse breed is famous, and horse racing is a passion here. The landscape north of town is open steppe, grassy in spring and dry in summer, stretching toward the border with Turkmenistan.

To the east, the Golestan National Park covers the forested slopes of the Alborz mountains, the Hyrcanian forest, a relic of ancient broadleaf woodland that is itself a World Heritage Site. The road through the park, between Golestan and Mashhad, winds through dense forest and is a beautiful ride, though busy with trucks.

The roads around Gonbad are generally good, flat on the steppe and twisting in the mountains. Traffic can be heavy, and driving standards demand constant attention. The climate is humid near the Caspian, drier on the steppe, and hot in summer.

Travel to Iran involves serious political and practical considerations for foreigners, including government advisories, banking restrictions and the need for a carnet for a foreign vehicle, so research carefully. The town of Gonbad-e Kavus can sort out fuel, food and a bed, and Azadshahr, nineteen kilometres away, is another option. Try local dishes such as the Turkmen flatbreads and lamb stews.
t.miandasht@36.4,56.1:
The map around Miandasht is a lot of space and not many names. This is the dry plain of north-eastern Iran, on the old Silk Road corridor that runs along the southern foot of the Alborz and connects the towns of Shahrud and Sabzevar and, beyond, the great oasis cities of Khorasan. The land is mostly steppe and salt flats, with low hills on the horizon, little water, and a big, pale sky. Mayamey, the nearest named place on our list, is the district to the west.

The name Miandasht means something like the middle of the plain, and in Iran it is linked with a caravanserai, one of the walled roadside inns that merchants used when they travelled by camel and mule. These buildings were built roughly a day's travel apart, so that a caravan could arrive before dark, water the animals, and sleep behind thick walls. Many date from the Safavid period, when the shahs put considerable effort into the road network, and a number are still standing in the open desert, their domes and arches turned to the colour of the soil. I cannot tell you exactly what stands at these coordinates, but the pattern of the region is that wherever the road crosses a long empty stretch, somebody built a place to stop.

For a rider, the interest is distance. The roads here are long, straight and often empty, the asphalt is generally decent on main routes and rougher on side roads, and the key problems are wind, heat in summer and the lack of services. Spring and autumn are the good seasons, with clear light and temperatures that do not punish. In the middle of the day the plain shimmers, so mirages are common, and you should check your fuel more often than you think you need to.

There are no towns on the list within reach, so plan fuel and water carefully, filling up in Shahrud or Sabzevar and carrying a spare bottle. Phone coverage can fade away in the open. Tell somebody where you are going, take more water than seems necessary, and stop to look at any old brick dome you pass.
t.mazinan@36.3,56.8:
Mazinān is a name I know from the map rather than from experience, a place on the dry plain of Khorasan in north-eastern Iran, between the desert edge and the foothills of the northern ranges, in the country west of Sabzevar. The label belongs to a ride that includes the caravanserai of Miandasht, and that tells you what kind of land this is: a section of the old Silk Road, where traders crossed the high plain with camels and mules between the Caspian region and the cities of the east. The caravanserais, walled inns built a day's travel apart, with a courtyard, stables and rooms around the edge, are among the most striking buildings in Iran, and the best survive as ruins of brick and mud.

The landscape is arid, a wide, gravelly plain with low ridges, dry riverbeds and patches of irrigated green where a qanat brings water to a village. Fields of wheat, melon and saffron are grown in places, and the air is dry and clear. At dawn and dusk the light on the hills turns pink and gold, and nights are cold. The silence is broad, and the sky is big. Spring brings a brief green to the steppe.

The road across the plain is straight and fast, with long distances between settlements, a mix of trucks, buses and local traffic, and the occasional herd of sheep or goats on the verge. The surface can be rough on minor roads, and the wind blows dust. Summer heat is severe, and winter nights can be freezing.

I cannot say what facilities lie exactly at this point, so assume nothing. Sabzevar, the nearest large town, has fuel, restaurants and hotels, and you should fill your tank there and carry water. Check the current rules for foreign visitors and for motorcycles before you plan this ride, because conditions can change. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.hyrcanian forests@37.4,55.7:
Fifty million years ago, forests like this covered much of the northern hemisphere, and in the Hyrcanian region they never entirely went away. A strip of woodland along the southern shore of the Caspian Sea, between the sea and the Alborz mountains, was sheltered from the ice ages by the water and the mountains, and it kept species that disappeared elsewhere. UNESCO recognised the Hyrcanian Forests in 2019, as a living relic of the temperate forests that once spread across Europe and Asia.

The forest is a thick one. Trees such as Persian ironwood, chestnut-leaved oak, hornbeam and Caucasian alder grow here, some of them hundreds of years old, and the undergrowth is full of ferns, mosses and wild pomegranate. The Caspian tiger, which lived in the reed beds and woods, was hunted to extinction in the twentieth century, but the Persian leopard survives in small numbers, together with brown bears, wolves, lynx and many birds. In autumn the leaves turn red and gold, and in spring the ground is carpeted in flowers.

The area around Kalaleh, in Golestan province, is where the forest meets the steppe. Kalaleh is the city of the Turkmen people, a Turkic community known for its horses, carpets and embroidery, and the weekly market is lively and colourful. The Turkmen steppe to the north is a flat, open country where horses graze, and the contrast between the dense forest and the open plain is striking. Golestan National Park, which includes much of the forest, is one of Iran's oldest reserves.

The roads that run through the park and over the mountains are narrow, steep and twisting, with sudden changes of weather. Mist and rain come off the Caspian, and the surface can be wet and slippery. It is a landscape for careful, patient riding, with plenty of stops for the view. Spring, when the forest is green and the flowers are out, and autumn are the best times. Summer is humid, and winter can be cold and snowy at height.

Kalaleh, twenty-one kilometres away, has thirty-four thousand people and is the place for fuel, food and basic services. Check local conditions and permits before entering protected areas.
t.mehr@36.3,57.1:
Mehr is one of those names that turns up in half a dozen places across Iran, because it means kindness or the sun, and in the old calendar it is also a month. This one lies in the north-east, in the broad plains of Khorasan between Sabzevar and the road towards Mashhad, a country of wheat, saffron, pistachio and long pale ridges where the Alborz tails off into the great deserts. It is a place for riding rather than sightseeing, and the pairing with Miandasht in the ride titles is a clue about why.

This was Silk Road land. The caravan trade between China, Central Asia and the Mediterranean passed along this corridor for well over a thousand years, and the Safavid shahs of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries built caravanserais along it, big fortified courtyards where a merchant and his animals could rest behind thick walls. Miandasht has one of these, and at its best it is a magnificent brick square with a high entrance and rooms around the inside. Stand in the courtyard at dusk and you can almost hear the camels.

The riding itself is straightforward and beautiful in a long, undramatic way. Roads run dead straight to a far vanishing point, then bend gently round a spur, and you are on the move again. Traffic is mostly trucks and the odd pickup loaded with melons or sheep. Winter is cold on this high plateau, with frost and sometimes snow, and summer is hot and dry, so spring and autumn are the seasons I would choose. Wind comes up in the afternoon, and cross-gusts out on the open stretches ask for attention.

Fuel here is not as frequent as in the west. Sabzevar and Mashhad are real cities with plenty of pumps, but between them you should not let the tank drop below half. Roadside tea houses and small restaurants do skewers, rice and yoghurt, and you will probably be asked in for tea even if you only meant to check your map.

I cannot tell you a lot about the village itself, and I would rather say so than invent it. Take it as a point on a great old trade road and go and look for the caravanserai, because that is where the history sits.
t.golestan@37.3,55.8:
Golestan means garden of roses in Persian, and the province that bears the name stretches from the Caspian shore across the plain to the foothills of the Alborz. At these coordinates, you are in the part of it where the land climbs toward the edge of the national park that takes its name from the province, the oldest national park in Iran, established in the 1950s and now a biosphere reserve. What makes it special is the sudden change: the park's western end is wet, green Hyrcanian forest, and as you travel east, the trees give way to drier woodland, then open steppe and semi-desert, a transition crammed into a short distance.

The wildlife benefits from this diversity. Leopards, brown bears, wolves, wild boar, red deer and the elusive Persian cheetah in the drier fringes have all been recorded in the wider area, though a rider will see little more than birds, and perhaps a deer at dusk. Spring is the time for wildflowers and migrant birds, and autumn colours fill the forest with copper and gold.

The nearest town is Kalaleh, a market town of over thirty thousand people on the plain, with petrol stations, shops, simple restaurants and guesthouses. Gonbad-e Qabus, a larger city a short distance west, is famous for the Gonbad-e Qabus tower, a ten-storey brick tower from the year 1006, rising about seventy metres on a mound, and one of the great early masterpieces of Islamic architecture. The Turkmen community here are renowned for weaving carpets and for raising horses, and the weekly markets are worth a stop.

Riding in the park area means winding roads through forest, with good surface in places but also sections of gravel and rough tarmac. Rain can arrive suddenly, particularly in spring, and the roads become slippery and muddy. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons. In summer the plain is hot and humid, while the high ground offers cooler air.

Rules apply inside the park, and permits or ranger approval may be required for certain tracks, so ask in advance. Fuel should be filled in Kalaleh or Gonbad before going in, since there is none inside the park boundary. Carry water, snacks and warm clothes, because weather changes quickly.
t.northland bay of islands weekend high po:
South of Auckland the motorway climbs over the Bombay Hills, a low line of old volcanic cones that marks the edge of the city's influence and the beginning of the Waikato. These coordinates sit in the rolling country below them, near Pukekohe East, and the soils here are among the richest in New Zealand, red-brown volcanic loam that grows potatoes, onions and vegetables for the whole country. Market gardens stretch across the paddocks, and in season, roadside stalls sell produce by the sack.

The hills themselves are not very high, rising to only a couple of hundred metres, but they have long been a boundary. In the 1860s they marked the line beyond which Māori tribes defended their territory during the Waikato war, and the story of those years is told in small museums and memorials. Pukekohe, a town of over twenty thousand, grew as a farming centre, and its racetrack is the place where the country's best motorsport drivers compete every year. Papakura, a little north, is a larger suburb of Auckland with fuel, food and everything else.

The roads in the region are quiet country lanes, with low hills, gentle bends and good surfaces. They are not demanding, but they are pleasant, and the long views across the plain, with Pukekohe's market gardens laid out in patchwork, are impressive. Clouds roll in from the west, and the weather changes quickly, with showers and bright intervals in the same hour. Early morning is the best time, with fog in the hollows and low sun on the fields, while the afternoon brings tractors and farm trucks.

If you are coming from the north on State Highway 1, the Bombay Hills section is the first stretch where you can feel the change in landscape, with the road rising and the city dropping behind. It is a good place to check the tyres, drink some water and plan the rest of the ride. The Bay of Islands lies far to the north, an entire day's ride, so this is more of a pit stop than a destination, and the fuel stations at Pukekohe and Papakura are the best option.
t.northland bay of islands weekend scenic:
East of Papakura the farmland lifts into the Hunua Ranges, a rugged range of forested hills that supplies most of Auckland's drinking water. These coordinates lie in the foothills, near the town of Red Hill and the quiet valley of the Wairoa River, and the road that runs through the area is one of the nicer ways of leaving the city. The Wairoa winds through paddocks and pine plantations, with willows trailing in the water and cattle standing in the shallows.

The Hunua Ranges Regional Park is the main attraction, a large protected area of native forest that rises to nearly seven hundred metres. Walking tracks lead to waterfalls, including Hunua Falls, where the stream drops about thirty metres over volcanic rock into a pool that is a favourite swimming spot. The forest holds rare birds, such as kokako and kiwi, along with native frogs, bats and giant weta, and the dawn chorus here is something to hear. The dams in the hills supply water to the city, so there are restrictions on where you can walk and swim.

Clevedon, the nearest village to the north, is a pretty farming community with an old hall, a polo club and a market that draws crowds on Sundays. The riding is calm, with a series of long, easy bends and gentle hills that make for a relaxed run. Roads are narrow in places, with little shoulder and wet leaves in winter, so watch your speed. Heavy rain can bring slips and flooding in the valleys, and the weather in the hills is often cooler and cloudier than in the city.

Papakura, about ten kilometres away, has a population of twenty-eight thousand and offers a full range of fuel and food stops, and you should fill up there before heading into the hills. There are no stations in the ranges, and few shops. The Northland Bay of Islands ride finishes here, a long day's ride from the north, and the last kilometres through the Hunua countryside are a gentle, green end to the trip, with the lights of Auckland a glow on the horizon.
t.rotorua lakes and forest@-37.0,175.2:
Between Papakura and the Firth of Thames lies a long, flat shore known as the Seabird Coast, and these coordinates fall in the farmland behind it. The road that runs along the water, State Highway 25, is a quiet stretch with a very long view, and it makes an excellent route for a motorcyclist who wants to leave the motorways behind. The ride is named for Rotorua's lakes and forests, but the first part of the day is a mellow warm-up along the edge of the Firth.

The Firth of Thames is a wide, muddy bay, and its tidal flats attract huge flocks of migrating birds. Each spring, bar-tailed godwits arrive from Alaska after flying non-stop across the Pacific, one of the longest migrations in the animal kingdom, and thousands gather at the shorebird centre at Miranda to feed and rest. Pūkeko and herons stalk the paddocks, and the mangroves hold fernbirds. Miranda also has hot springs, with mineral pools that are a good place to rest. Kaiaua, a small beach village, is famous for fish and chips, and on a summer weekend there is often a queue.

The riding is relaxed. The coast road is generally straight and flat, with a few gentle bends and a good surface, and the main hazard is the weekend crowd and the strong westerly that can blow across the open land. In the early morning, with mist on the water and the sun rising over the Coromandel Range, the light is lovely. Be careful of the tidal flats, which have no barriers, and of horses and cyclists on the shoulder.

Fuel is the thing to plan for. There are stations at Papakura, about twenty-four kilometres from here, and at Pokeno and Thames, but the coast itself has few, and some close early. Fill up before you set out and carry some water. Food stops are friendly, with cafés and fish shops in the villages, and the Miranda shorebird centre has a small café. Rotorua is more than two hours' drive to the south, so this stretch is a gentle prelude to the volcanic country, with the Coromandel's blue hills on the horizon.
t.waitakere ranges and piha@-36.7,175.0:
Past the Hunua Ranges, between the Wairoa and Waikato valleys, the Auckland region ends, and these coordinates lie near its southern limit in the rolling farm country around Pukekohe. The ride that this belongs to is called Waitākere Ranges and Piha, and the ranges lie well to the north-west, a green, rain-soaked wall of hills that rises behind Auckland's west coast. So this is a long way from the surf, and the best use is as a place to refuel.

Pukekohe and its surrounding villages, with their market gardens and orchards, form a fertile belt that feeds the city. The soil is rich and dark, the gardens are busy all year and the roadside stalls sell sweetcorn, kumara and strawberries at prices that city shoppers dream of. In spring the paddocks are patched with the green of young crops and the purple of lupins. In winter the fields glisten with frost.

The reason to include the Waitākere Ranges on any itinerary is their wildness. They are a rugged, forested massif that holds the biggest tract of native bush in the Auckland region, and the road from Titirangi to Piha winds through it in a series of tight, shady bends. Kauri trees still stand there, though a disease known as kauri dieback has led to closures of many walking tracks and requires visitors to scrub their boots. At Piha, the black-sand beach is dominated by Lion Rock, a great volcanic plug that rises from the sand, and the surf is among the most famous in the country. The beach was also the setting for a popular television series about lifeguards.

For riders, the coastal roads are steep, narrow and often slippery with moss and leaf litter, so go slowly and watch for fallen branches, especially after rain. Fuel is a concern. Titirangi, on the eastern edge of the ranges, has a station, but the coast has none, so fill up before you go. Most of the reliable stations are in the bigger centres, such as Pukekohe and Papakura, a fair distance away. Mist can fill the valleys in the early morning, and the road can be cold and damp even in summer.
t.waitakere ranges and piha high point@-37:
The Hunua Ranges are the green hills that you see from the southern motorway, rising behind Papakura like a breaking wave, and these coordinates sit in their folds, near Red Hill and the farm lanes of the Wairoa valley. The ranges are the highest ground in this part of Auckland, and the loftiest peak, Kohukohunui, reaches close to seven hundred metres. From some of the lookouts you can see across the Hauraki Gulf to the Coromandel and, on a clear day, to the volcanic cones of the Auckland isthmus.

The ranges are a regional park, protected for their bush and for the dams that store most of the city's water. Pest control has brought back kokako, one of the rarest forest birds in the country, whose haunting, organ-like song carries through the trees. Walkers climb to waterfalls and lookouts, and the forest, with its tree ferns, rimu and kauri, is thick and moist. Heavy rain can send brown torrents down the streams, and fallen trees block the tracks, so check conditions before you go.

The roads at the edge of the ranges have few equals near the city. Hunua Road climbs and drops through patches of bush and farmland, with tight bends and stretches of rough, patched tar. It is narrow, and the edge is soft in places, and there are blind corners where cattle trucks and logging rigs appear without warning. Do not expect a high-speed thrill, but do expect a pleasant, leafy ride on a quiet morning. In the late afternoon, the sun slants through the trees and picks out the ferns in gold.

Fuel is the thing to remember. Papakura, about thirteen kilometres away, is the nearest big town, and Takanini, a little north, has several stations. There is nothing in the ranges, and the little community of Hunua has only a small store. Bring a coat, because the hills are often cooler than the plain, and pack some lunch if you plan a long day. The ride that includes this point begins with the climb and ends at the sea, and it is the climb that stays in the mind.
t.waitakere ranges and piha scenic road@-3:
These coordinates fall in the Hauraki Gulf, between the North Shore and the island of Waiheke, in water that Aucklanders cross by ferry and yacht, and nothing here is a road. But the gulf is the thing that makes Auckland what it is, and it is worth a thought as you plan a ride that ends at Piha on the opposite coast.

Waiheke, the nearest island, is a short ferry ride from the city and has become a destination for its vineyards, olive groves and beaches. Its wines, particularly the reds, have won prizes abroad, and the cellar doors and restaurants on its hillsides draw visitors in numbers every summer. Cars and motorcycles can go over on the vehicle ferry, and the island's roads are narrow, winding and hilly, with bends that reward a careful rider. Rangitoto, the almost symmetrical volcanic cone beside the harbour mouth, erupted only about six hundred years ago, and its black lava fields are now covered in pōhutukawa and scrub.

On the mainland side, Pakuranga, a suburb of Howick, has about nine thousand people and the fuel and food stops that go with them, and the nearby village of Howick has an open-air historical village that recreates the lives of the Fencible soldiers who settled the area in the 1840s. The roads here are busy and suburban, with traffic lights and roundabouts, and it takes a determined effort to get out to the quiet country. Weekday mornings are slow, and the motorway can be jammed in both directions.

The reward comes when you leave the city. West of Auckland, the Waitākere Ranges rise in a wall of green, and the road to Piha, with its hairpins and tunnels of tree ferns, is one of the finest in the region. Take care in the wet, because moss and leaf litter make the surface slick, and the shade can hide frost in winter. On a clear evening, the sunset over the Tasman, with the Lion Rock black against the sky, makes a fitting end to a day's riding.
t.auckland new zealand@-37.0,175.3:
The Firth of Thames is a broad, shallow arm of the Hauraki Gulf, and these coordinates sit on its western shore, in the flat country where the Hauraki Plains meet the water. Thames, the nearest town, lies at the southern end, and behind it the Coromandel Range rises in a long, dark, bushy wall. It is a landscape of wide skies and low light, with the tide drawing off across the mudflats and the hills turning from green to blue as the day wears on.

Thames was a gold town.
