In 1867 prospectors found rich quartz reefs in the hills above, and within a few years the population exploded, with dozens of batteries crushing ore day and night and hotels lining the main street. The boom did not last, but the buildings of that era, solid and elaborate, still stand in the old streets, and the School of Mines, with its collection of minerals and mining equipment, tells the story. The town now has seven thousand people and a relaxed, slightly faded air, with good cafés and a small market.

North from Thames, State Highway 25 follows the coast, a narrow and winding road that hugs the shore beneath huge old pōhutukawa trees that lean out over the water. In December they burst into crimson bloom, and the road is lined with red. The surface is generally good, but the bends are tight, the verge is narrow and the sea is close on one side and the cliff on the other. Inland, the Kauaeranga Valley road runs to the foot of the Pinnacles, a jagged volcanic ridge that is the goal of a famous day walk, with a hut at the top for those who want to see the sunrise.

Fuel and food are easy in Thames, which is about twenty-two kilometres away, and the small villages along the coast have cafés and shops, but stations are rare and some close early. Ngatea, on the plains to the south, is smaller, and Coromandel, a long ride north, is a good place to stop for the night. A swim is possible at several beaches on the coast road, though the Firth is muddy and the water is better on the eastern side of the peninsula. Fog can lie on the plains in the early morning, and summer holiday weekends bring a lot of traffic.
t.east cape long adventure@-37.2,175.1:
There is a patch of quiet country east of Pukekohe and south of the Hunua Ranges, where the roads wander between paddocks and pine plantations, and these coordinates fall in the middle of it. It is not a place with a famous name, but it is the kind of land that fills the space between Auckland and the Waikato, and it makes a very decent place to eat and rest before a long day eastward.

The Hunua countryside is dairy and lifestyle farming, with a sprinkling of orchards, paddocks of horses and stands of exotic trees. The roads here are slow and bendy, with one-lane bridges over small streams and a string of country halls where the community gathers for dances and fairs. The ranges to the north are thick with native bush, and the sound of bellbirds and tui drifts from the trees. In the early morning, with mist in the hollows and cows steaming in the cold, the landscape has an almost English softness.

The ride that takes in this point is called the East Cape Long Adventure, and the name is accurate. The East Cape is a remote peninsula at the north-eastern corner of the North Island, a place of rolling green hills, empty beaches and small Māori communities, and a long way from anywhere. The road around it, State Highway 35, runs for more than three hundred kilometres past tiny marae, whitewashed churches and rows of pōhutukawa, and ends near the lighthouse at the easternmost point of the country, which is reached by climbing about seven hundred steps. The journey east from here crosses the Hauraki Plains, passes through Waihi with its gold mine and drops to the Bay of Plenty, so it is a long first leg.

Pukekohe East, about sixteen kilometres from here, is the nearest town of any size, with plenty of fuel and food, and Papakura is another good option. In the countryside, stations are few and cafés are rare, so eat before you go, and bring a jacket. The weather in the ranges changes quickly, with fog in the morning and showers in the afternoon, and winter evenings come early. At the end of the day the sky over the hills turns a deep orange, and the smell of cut grass and woodsmoke hangs in the air.
t.whitianga beach@-36.8,175.7:
Mercury Bay is the name on the map, and Whitianga is the town that wraps around it, on the eastern side of the Coromandel Peninsula where the Pacific comes in flat and blue and rather unhurried. Captain Cook anchored here in November 1769 to watch the transit of Mercury, which is how the bay got its name, and Māori ancestors had been using the harbour long before that. The beach in front of the town is a long, gentle curve of pale sand with shallow water, the sort of beach where you can leave your jacket and boots on a bag and actually swim without negotiating surf.

You get here on State Highway 25, which on this peninsula is a road with opinions. From Thames it crawls up the Firth of Thames shore under old pōhutukawa trees, then cuts across the ranges, climbing through bush with tight, damp bends where the surface changes colour with every patch of shade. Early in the morning the corners are cool and slick under the ferns, and by afternoon the camper vans have woken up, so I would ride the hills early and keep the beach for later. Gravel on the apexes is a regular feature after rain, and it rains with enthusiasm on the Coromandel.

Whitianga itself is easy. With a population of a little over three thousand it has fuel in town, cafes along the waterfront, and a small passenger ferry that crosses to Ferry Landing on the Kuaotunu side if you feel like a pointless but charming minute on the water. Coromandel town, about twenty kilometres up the coast, is the next real stop for supplies, and Tairua is a similar hop south. Thames, thirty-odd kilometres back, is the larger town with the bigger supermarkets and mechanics if something needs attention.

The reason to linger is the coast itself. A short drive from town you get Cathedral Cove and Hot Water Beach, where at low tide people dig their own spa pits in the sand above a geothermal spring, and both are busy in summer and almost empty in winter. Scallops are a local pride, and the fish and chip shops tend to be worth their reputation. Come between late spring and early autumn if you want warm water, but I like the shoulder months, when the light is low and golden over the bay and you can park the bike with nobody to apologise to.
t.sigatoka@-18.1,177.5:
Sigatoka is the town where the Queens Road crosses the river of the same name, on the southern coast of Viti Levu, Fiji's main island. The river valley behind it is known as the Salad Bowl of Fiji, a fertile strip of farmland where vegetables, taro and other crops are grown and trucked to the markets and resorts along the coast. On any given day, the town's market is full of piled-up pineapples, cassava, chilli and bundles of kava root, and it is a good place to watch ordinary Fijian life in motion.

For a rider, the Queens Road here is easy and enjoyable. It follows the coast with low hills on one side and the reef-fringed sea on the other, the surface is generally good, and the traffic moves at a relaxed pace. Fijians drive on the left, as in Britain, and village speed limits are low, with speed bumps at the entrance to most settlements, often unmarked until you hit them. Dogs, children, horses and cows are all part of the road. Rain comes in sudden tropical downpours, the best weather is generally from May to October, and the sun can be punishing, so cover up and drink plenty of water.

Just west of the town the Sigatoka Sand Dunes National Park runs along the coast, a ridge of windblown sand up to about sixty metres high, and an unexpected place to find ancient burial sites. Archaeologists have found pottery and human remains there that are thousands of years old, among the earliest evidence of settlement in the islands. Further up the valley, the old hill fort at Tavuni, built by a Tongan chief, shows how contested these lands once were. You can reach it by road from the river valley.

Sigatoka is the biggest town on this stretch of coast, with banks, supermarkets, a hospital and several fuel stations, so it is a proper place to fill up and eat. The Coral Coast resorts begin just east of here, and Nadi, with its airport, lies roughly forty kilometres to the north-west. Try a lunch of fresh fish in coconut milk, or a roti, a flatbread wrap that reflects the Indo-Fijian community, and a cold drink from a street stall.
t.coral coast@-18.2,177.6:
The Coral Coast is the name given to the stretch of southern Viti Levu between Sigatoka and Pacific Harbour, and the name is earned. A fringing reef runs along most of the shoreline, a few hundred metres out, and at low tide you can see the pale shapes of coral heads through shallow, clear water. Behind it, dark green hills rise toward the interior, covered in forest and sugar cane and cut by short streams that rush down to the sea. This is the leeward side of the island, so it gets less rain than the east, and the weather is usually kinder.

The Queens Road runs the length of it, and it is a very easy road. The surface is mostly sealed and good, the corners are lazy and rolling, and the sea glints at the edge of the view every few minutes. It is not a road for speed, and the traffic of buses, trucks and local cars moves at its own gentle pace. Every village has speed bumps, and you will pass school children in neat uniforms, men carrying machetes and women selling fruit from roadside stalls. Slow down, wave, and you will get a lot of waves and the word bula, the Fijian greeting, in return.

Life here is built around the villages and the sea. Many villages own the fishing rights to the reef in front of them, and traditions still matter. If you are invited into a village, accept with modesty. Shoulders and knees should be covered, hats are usually removed, and a gift of kava root is the traditional courtesy. Several resorts along the coast welcome day visitors for lunch and a swim, and the snorkelling over the reef is excellent. A small wildlife park near Sigatoka shows some of Fiji's native species, including native birds and the banded iguana.

There is no single stopping point on the Coral Coast, because the whole length is the experience. Fuel stations are found in Sigatoka and the larger centres, with only occasional small pumps between, so top up when you have the chance. Shops in the villages sell cold drinks and snacks, and fruit stalls offer pineapple, mango and coconut. Late afternoon, when the light turns gold and the sea flattens, is the best time to be on the road.
t.pacific harbour@-18.2,178.1:
Pacific Harbour is a planned resort development, laid out in the 1970s on a swampy stretch of the southern coast, with canals, golf fairways and neat lots, and it has since settled into being Fiji's self-styled adventure capital. The name is a little grander than the place, but the setting is real. A broad lagoon sits offshore, sheltered by the reef, and beyond it the island of Beqa rises in a green hump. It is a good-looking, quiet, slightly theatrical spot, and it makes an easy overnight between Suva and the Coral Coast.

The ride here along the Queens Road from the west brings a gradual change. East of the Coral Coast the climate becomes wetter, the vegetation thicker, and the sky heavier with cloud, because this side of Viti Levu catches the trade winds. Rain is common and sometimes heavy, so waterproofs are sensible at any time of year. The road itself is generally well kept, with gentle curves through coconut palms and forest, plus the usual hazards of dogs, speed bumps and slow trucks. The distance from Suva is about forty kilometres, an easy morning's ride.

Beqa Lagoon is the headline attraction for divers. It is famous for shark dives where several species, including bull sharks and, with luck, tiger sharks, are drawn by feeding in a marine reserve, and it has made Pacific Harbour a name in the diving world. On land, the Navua River runs close by, and boat trips run up its gorge through rainforest and waterfalls. The island of Beqa is also the home of the traditional firewalking ceremony, in which men walk across heated stones without injury, and performances are sometimes given for visitors at local hotels.

Pacific Harbour has the services a rider needs: a few shops, restaurants, a small fuel option and accommodation, though Suva, the capital, has the main supply of everything and is the place to fill up fully. Fresh seafood is excellent here, and a meal of grilled fish with cassava and a cold local beer is hard to improve on. Keep an eye on the sky, and if you are caught in a downpour, wait it out under a shop awning with a hot cup of tea.
t.rangipo desert@-39.3,175.7:
Rangipo is called a desert, and it is not one. It is a high volcanic plateau in the centre of the North Island, lying in the rain shadow of the volcanoes, so that it gets far less rain than the land around it, and its soils are poor, stony and fast-draining. The result is a bleak, wide landscape of tussock, red-brown scrub and black lava gravel, with the cone of Ruapehu rising to the west and the long ridge of Kaimanawa to the east. It is a place of long horizons and heavy skies, and the road across it, the Desert Road, is one of the best-known in New Zealand.

State Highway 1 climbs here to about 1,074 metres, the highest point on the national highway network, and it can be dramatic. In summer the road is dry and fast, with long, gentle bends and open views, and the wind can be fierce, especially from the west. In winter it is a different story. Snow, ice and sudden whiteouts close the road without much notice, and drivers sometimes spend hours waiting for it to reopen. Check the road status before you set out, carry warm clothing and chains if appropriate, and do not trust a clear morning in Taupo to predict what you will find on top.

Much of the land on the east side of the road is a military training area, used by the New Zealand Defence Force, and you will see signs warning of live firing and unexploded ordnance, and warning you to stay on the road. Do not stray into it. The tussock and scrub shelter a number of rare plants and insects, and the area is protected for its conservation value, in contrast to its bleak appearance. Native falcons hunt over the plain, and the sky at night is clear and full of stars.

Services are few. Waiouru, at the southern end, is a small town with about 1,300 people, an army museum and some fuel and food. Turangi, to the north, is a bit bigger and has more, and it is wise to fill up at one or the other before you start the crossing. There are a few lay-bys but no shops on the road itself. Long straight sections tempt drivers to speed, and the police are known to watch this stretch, so keep to the limits and enjoy the scenery.
t.mount ruapehu view@-39.2,175.6:
Ruapehu is the highest mountain in the North Island, at 2,797 metres, and one of the most active volcanoes in New Zealand, and from the Desert Road it fills the western sky with a long white ridge and a dark, jagged crater rim. Its snow-covered flanks glow pink at dawn and dusk. It has three main peaks and a lake in its crater that is warm, acidic and, at times, very hot, and the volcano erupted violently in 1995 and 1996, throwing ash across the island. Alongside it, to the north, rise the more perfect cone of Ngāuruhoe, which stood in for Mount Doom in the Lord of the Rings films, and the broken top of Tongariro.

For Māori the mountains are sacred, ancestors and guardians of the land. A legend tells that they were once warriors in a great battle for the love of a mountain called Pihanga, and that Taranaki, the loser, fled west to the sea. The area is a dual World Heritage Site, listed for both its natural and its cultural values. Today the slopes hold two big ski areas, Whakapapa and Turoa, which fill with skiers from June until October.

The view from the road is best when the weather is clear, which it often is not. Cloud sits on the mountain for days at a time, and the peak reveals itself only in short glimpses. When it does, the sight is worth a pause at a lay-by. On the ride itself, the road is smooth and gently curved, with long views over the plateau. Wind from the west can be strong, and the temperature can drop fast. Take warm gear and be prepared for snow in any season but midsummer.

A sad place lies not far to the south-west: Tangiwai, where on Christmas Eve 1953 a lahar from the crater lake swept away a railway bridge just before a night express arrived, and 151 people died. A memorial stands beside the road and a visit is sobering. The nearest fuel is at Waiouru, to the south, and Turangi, to the north, both small towns with services, so check your tank before you set off. Take food and a hot drink, and linger if the clouds part, for the mountain does not always oblige.
t.cathedral cove@-36.8,175.8:
Cathedral Cove is a sea arch on the east coast of the Coromandel Peninsula, a high, pale tunnel of volcanic rock cut by the waves, which links two small beaches and frames the sea like a window. It stands within a marine reserve, and the water around it is clear, with rocks and kelp beds that attract fish and snorkellers. The cliffs above are crowned with the red flowers of pōhutukawa, the New Zealand Christmas tree, which bloom in December and give the coast a blaze of colour. The arch itself is vast, high enough to hold a house, and the sand underfoot is soft and white.

The way to it is a walk, not a ride, from a car park above Hahei, and the walk takes about forty-five minutes each way on a path with steps and a few hills. The track has been damaged by storms and slips in recent years, so check its status with the Department of Conservation before you set out. Do not expect to ride down, and leave your gear locked and out of sight at the car park. In summer the track and beach are crowded, so go early or late, when the light is softer and the sand is quiet. The cove was used in the Narnia films, and it appears in many a postcard.

The road to Hahei from Whitianga is a pleasure, a twisting coastal road through farmland and bush, with views of the bay and small islands, and a good surface. It has tight bends and some steep sections, and the traffic in summer can be slow, with caravans and holiday cars. Rain can make the road slippery, and the verges are soft. Take your time, enjoy the view, and keep an eye on the weather, which can change fast on this coast.

Close by is Hot Water Beach, where hot springs rise through the sand at low tide, and visitors dig their own pools in the sand, an experience that is best arranged around the tides. Whitianga, about thirty minutes away, has fuel, shops and a choice of places to eat, and Hahei has a few cafés and a shop, though prices are higher in summer. Fill the tank in Whitianga before you set out. If you stay the night, you will wake to the sound of surf and birds.
t.tairua@-37.0,175.9:
Tairua sits at the mouth of a tidal estuary on the east coast of the Coromandel Peninsula, a small, easy-going town beneath a dome of volcanic rock called Mount Paku. The mountain is the remnant of an old volcano, a steep, bush-covered hump about 179 metres high, and a short walking track leads to the top, where a viewing platform looks out over the estuary, the town and the Pacific. On a clear day, you can see a line of small islands offshore, and the long beaches stretching both ways. It is a modest climb, and a good one for a rider who wants to get off the bike and see where he is.

Across the water is Pauanui, a twin town built in the 1960s as a holiday resort, with canals and boat moorings, and a passenger ferry links the two in summer. Tairua itself is older, with a small harbour, a wharf where fishing boats tie up, and a main street of cafés and shops. The Māori name is said to mean two tides, a nod to the way the estuary has water coming in from two directions, and legend holds that the great Arawa canoe visited here on its voyage from Hawaiki. Kauri logs were once floated down the river from the hills to the harbour, a trade that shaped the early European settlement.

The riding on the way in, along State Highway 25, is a joy. The road runs between the hills and the sea, with plenty of bends, good surface and views of beaches and bays. It is well used, so slow vehicles and holiday traffic are common, but passing places are frequent. In wet weather the road is slippery, and in summer it fills with campervans and cars. The scenery is lovely, with forest, farmland and glimpses of the sea, and the pōhutukawa in the roadside bush are a sight in December.

Tairua is a handy place to stop for fuel, food and a rest. The town has a petrol station, a supermarket, bakeries and cafés serving good coffee and fresh fish, and a few places to stay. Whangamata to the south and Thames to the west are larger, but there is rarely any need to go that far. The beach at Tairua is wide and gentle, and a swim on a warm day is a fine reward after a morning in the saddle.
t.bourg murat@-21.2,55.6:
Bourg-Murat is a roadside village on the high plateau between Réunion's coast and its volcano, and it is a place of mist, cattle and the smell of wet grass. The altitude is felt immediately: after the warm, humid coast the air is cool, often cloudy, and in winter you may even see frost. The Plaine des Cafres, which surrounds the village, is dairy country, with green pastures, cows and farms, and it feels oddly like the highlands of Europe on a tropical island.

The main reason to stop is the Cité du Volcan, a museum on the edge of the village devoted to the Piton de la Fournaise, which is one of the most active volcanoes in the world. It erupts every year or two, usually in the uninhabited summit area, and lava often flows down to the sea on the east coast where the road gets crossed by black rock. The museum is a good place to learn how the island was built and what to do when an eruption occurs, and the cafés nearby are warm refuges when the weather turns.

The Route du Volcan climbs from here through a landscape of forest and heath, and it becomes steadily wilder. The road is well maintained, with smooth tarmac and long, steady bends, but it is a mountain road and the weather can change quickly, with fog and sudden rain. Mornings are best for clear views of the volcano and the surrounding peaks, and by afternoon cloud usually rolls in. In winter it can be bitingly cold, so bring layers and waterproofs.

Practicalities are easy here. Le Tampon, the large town about ten kilometres down the slope, has petrol stations, supermarkets and everything you might need, and some fuel is usually available along the main road in the plains villages as well. Fill up before you climb to the volcano, because there is nothing beyond. Food in Bourg-Murat is typically Creole: rice, beans, rougail sausage and chicken curry, along with the local cheese and yoghurt from the dairy farms. A sweet bread or a bowl of soup hits the spot on a chilly day.

Réunion is a French department, so euros are used and French is spoken, along with Creole. A friendly bonjour goes a long way.
t.plaine des sables@-21.2,55.6:
Nothing prepares you for the Plaine des Sables. Climb out of the forest on the Route du Volcan and the world turns to rust, ash and black cinder, a plain of broken volcanic gravel at around two thousand metres that looks like Mars or the Moon, depending on who is telling the story. Space agencies have actually used landscapes like this to test equipment. Scattered cones rise from the plain, red and black and brown, and not a tree grows on it.

It was made by the Piton de la Fournaise, which sits at the end of the road and is still one of the most active volcanoes on the planet. Over thousands of years, its eruptions have dropped ash and scoria across the plateau, and the wind and rain have worked on them since. The colours shift with the light: pink at dawn, silver at midday, and a deep red-brown when the cloud shadows pass. There is often a strange silence, interrupted only by wind, and a smell of wet stone. Hardy plants such as heather-like shrubs and small orange lichens grow in the cracks, and the occasional bird of prey circles above.

The ride across is easy, with a smooth road through a landscape that has almost no other vehicles, and hardly any bends to speak of before the final climb. But the conditions are demanding. Cloud arrives with little warning, visibility can drop to a few metres, and the temperature falls sharply at this height. In wet weather the road can be slick, and wind across the open plain can push a bike. Go early in the morning if you can, when the air is clear and the plain is empty.

There are no services at all on the plain. Le Tampon, fifteen kilometres or more behind you, is the place to fill the tank and buy water and food, and the nearest cafés are back in Bourg-Murat. Carry warm layers, rain gear, water and a charged phone.

At the end of the road a viewpoint looks down into the huge crater of the Enclos Fouqué, and on clear days you can see the cone of the volcano itself, black and quiet and entirely worth the cold.
t.rotorua lakes@-37.0,175.2:
The point on the map falls in the rural country southeast of Auckland, between the sprawl of Papakura and the heights of the Hunua Ranges, an area of farmland, small vineyards and forested hills that most visitors never see. Auckland ends here rather suddenly, with the last houses giving way to paddocks, cattle, hedges of macrocarpa and the occasional lifestyle block. The Hunua Ranges, a large regional park, hold some of the city's water supply and the remnants of native forest, with the Hunua Falls and tracks to waterfalls.

The ride this belongs to heads southeast to Rotorua, about two hundred and thirty kilometres away, through the Waikato and the Bay of Plenty. Rotorua is built on a volcanic caldera and filled with geothermal activity, with steaming vents, bubbling mud pools and the smell of sulphur drifting across town. It is also the heart of Te Arawa, a Māori tribe who settled the area some six hundred years ago, and traditional performances, food cooked in steam and carved meeting houses are all part of the experience. The lakes around, Rotorua, Tarawera, Okareka and others, are scenic, and the tall redwoods in the Whakarewarewa Forest were planted in 1901 as an experiment.

The start from here is far gentler than leaving the city centre. Narrow country roads wind through rolling pasture, and the traffic is local, with tractors, stock trucks and weekend cyclists. The roads out toward the Firth of Thames and the Coromandel are twisty and bumpy, with views over the mudflats, and mist often lies in the valleys at dawn. Rain can be heavy, and gravel on bends is common, so keep a cautious pace. Autumn and spring are mild, and summer is warm and dry.

Fuel is available at Papakura, about twenty-four kilometres away, and the neighbouring suburbs, and there are small stations in country villages, but they close early, so fill in town. The big roads to the south, State Highway 1 and the Waikato Expressway, are fast and busy, with services at regular intervals.

Pick up a meat pie at a country bakery, a New Zealand tradition, and look at the hills in the early light.
t.taumarunui@-38.9,175.3:
Taumarunui is a railway and river town in the middle of the North Island, in the hill country that people call the King Country. The name comes from the Māori King Movement, whose leaders took refuge here in the nineteenth century when the land was closed to the colonial government. The Whanganui and Ongarue rivers meet nearby, and the Whanganui, long a canoe highway, flows south from here through deep bush to the sea. The main trunk railway from Auckland to Wellington passes through, and the town grew as a railway stop, with a main street that still has the look of that busy age.

It is also the start of the Forgotten World Highway, State Highway 43, a long and extraordinary road across empty farmland and forest to Stratford in Taranaki, around 150 kilometres. The road climbs over three saddles, through steep gorges and old tunnels, past tiny settlements and farms that look as though the clock stopped. The most famous stop is Whangamomona, a village that declared itself a republic in 1989 after a boundary change, and its old hotel and its passport stamp are part of the fun. The Moki Tunnel is a rough, narrow bore through the hill, and a stretch of the road near Tangarakau is unsealed gravel, so you must watch the surface and reduce your speed.

The riding is slow, twisty and big on character. The bends are tight and often damp, there are few barriers, and the scenery of papa clay hills, tree ferns and sheep paddocks is greener than you expect. Rain is frequent, mist hangs in the gullies, and a cold morning can be icy in the shade, so set off warm and expect to take longer than the distance suggests. Livestock sometimes wander on the road, and wild goats are not unknown.

Fuel is the thing to settle first. Taumarunui is a town of a few thousand with petrol stations and food, and the highway beyond has long gaps with very little in the way of supplies, so fill the tank here and carry something to eat. Stratford is the next proper town on the far side. To the east you can see the snow on Mount Ruapehu on a clear day, a reminder that the volcanic plateau is close.
t.zlatoust@55.2,59.7:
Zlatoust lies in a valley between ridges of the southern Urals, about two hundred thousand people packed along the Ai river, and it is one of the most distinctive industrial towns in the mountains. The name means golden-mouthed, a translation of the epithet of Saint John Chrysostom, and the town was founded in the eighteenth century around an ironworks. It sits in a landscape of steep forested slopes and cold clear rivers, and the weather is often changeable, with mist and rain on the ridges.

The town is famed for steel. In the nineteenth century, a German-trained master began producing swords and knives in the town, and engraved steel weapons with beautiful decoration became its speciality. The Zlatoust arms factory, established in the early nineteenth century, made blades for the Russian army, and the craft of etching and gilding steel, with pictures of hunting scenes and landscapes, is still alive. The museum in town displays remarkable examples, and you can see how much skill went into the work.

From the town, mountains rise on every side. The Taganay National Park, just to the west, protects a range of quartzite peaks with rocky ridges, boulder fields and mossy forest, and the summit of Mount Taganay, at about 1,100 metres, offers a wide view over the Urals. A road leads close to the base, and well-marked trails climb the final stretch. Further on, Lake Zyuratkul, a cold, deep mountain lake surrounded by forest at high altitude, is a popular place for walking and for quiet camping. Satka, a small town to the west, is known for its magnesite quarries and the old Urals iron industry.

The main highway crosses the Urals near here, following the railway through the mountains. It is a road of long climbs and descents, with plenty of heavy trucks, and the weather can be wild on the passes, with fog, rain and early snow. Side roads climb through the forest on narrower tarmac, with short steep sections and bends.

Zlatoust has fuel stations, repair shops, supermarkets and cafés, and it makes a practical stop for a night. Local food includes dumplings, pickled vegetables and fish pies. The best months are June to September, and autumn is lovely when the birches turn yellow, though snow can arrive early in the hills.
t.perm@58.0,56.3:
Perm lies on the Kama river, the great tributary of the Volga, on the western slopes of the Urals, and it is a city that has given its name to a whole chapter of the earth's history. When the British geologist Roderick Murchison travelled through the region in the 1840s, he found rocks and fossils from a period he had not seen before and called it the Permian, after the old province of Perm. That period, which ended with the largest mass extinction ever recorded, is now known across the world.

The city itself was founded in 1723 as a copper smelting works at Yagoshikha, and it grew into a major industrial centre, producing guns, ships and machinery. About a million people live here, and it has a cultural life out of proportion to its location. The Perm Opera and Ballet Theatre has a long tradition, going back to the days when Sergei Diaghilev, the founder of the Ballets Russes, spent his childhood in the town. The writer Boris Pasternak lived here in 1916 and 1917 and drew on it in Doctor Zhivago, where it appears as the city of Yuryatin.

The Kama is a wide, slow river, and the embankment in the city is a pleasant place for a walk, with views of the long bridges and the river traffic. Perm is also known for its wooden sculpture, a tradition from the old Komi-Permyak culture, in which strangely expressive figures of saints and gods were carved from logs. A museum in an old church shows these carvings, and they are worth the visit.

To the east and south, the land rises toward the Ural foothills, with forested ridges, limestone cliffs and caves. Kungur, about ninety kilometres southeast, has a famous ice cave, and the road to it passes through rolling farmland and forest. Further east, the road to Usva and Gubakha climbs into the Urals proper, with rocky river gorges and pine woods. The surfaces vary, and trucks are heavy on the main routes. Frost heaves and potholes appear in spring.

Everything you need for a ride is in Perm, including fuel, workshops and hotels. The traffic in the centre is dense, so avoid rush hours. The local cuisine is hearty, with fish pies, dumplings and mushroom dishes. Summers are warm and short, autumn colours arrive in September, and winters are cold and snowy.
t.kauaeranga valley@-37.1,175.6:
The Kauaeranga Valley runs up from the edge of Thames into the steep, wooded core of the Coromandel Peninsula, and it tells the story of the region more honestly than the postcard beaches on the other coast. Thames, about six and a half kilometres away, was a gold-rush town in 1867, and when the gold gave out the loggers turned to the great kauri forests. The valley is full of reminders. Dams built of kauri logs were used to hold water and release it in a flood to float timber down to the mill, and the remains of one, the Dancing Camp dam, can still be walked to.

Today the valley is a forest park, with the Department of Conservation visitor centre a short way up the road. The land is rugged, with volcanic ridges, rocky pinnacles and dense bush, and the road runs beside a clear stream through steep walls of green. Beyond the visitor centre the road narrows and the surface gets rougher, ending at trailheads for the Pinnacles, a famous walk to a rocky summit with a hut where trampers stay overnight. The trees are a mix of regenerating kauri, rimu and tree ferns, and the air smells of wet earth and leaf litter.

For a rider, this is a short, rewarding detour rather than a long road. The valley road is narrow and winding, with single-lane bridges, shaded corners and sometimes gravel. Rain can fall hard here and the stream rises, so check conditions before you commit. State Highway 25, the main road along the Firth of Thames, has lovely views over the water but is busy on summer weekends with holiday traffic and the odd campervan. Early morning is the best time, with mist on the hills and little traffic.

Practically, Thames, with about seven thousand people, has fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and a long main street of old verandahed buildings, and it is the last sure place for services on this side of the peninsula. Tairua on the east coast, with fifteen hundred or so residents, is the next town. Carry water and a rain jacket, and leave time to stop at the visitor centre to learn a bit more about the forest.
t.nadi@-17.8,177.4:
Nadi is the town most visitors see first, because the international airport sits right beside it, and it tends to be judged a little unfairly as a gateway rather than a place. But it has real character, with a large Indo-Fijian community whose ancestors came as indentured labourers to work the sugar cane in the nineteenth century, and the main street smells of curry, incense and diesel. The Sri Siva Subramaniya Swami Temple, a brightly painted Hindu temple with an enormous carved gopuram tower, is the largest in the Southern Hemisphere and is open to visitors who take off their shoes and dress modestly.

Fuel, supermarkets, banks and repair shops are all easy here, and the population of around forty thousand makes it the main commercial centre of the west of Viti Levu. Nearby, the Garden of the Sleeping Giant has a large collection of orchids in the hills. A short ride away are the beaches of the Denarau resorts. Lautoka, eighteen kilometres to the north, is the sugar city, with a big mill, and the cane fields stretch across the plain in every direction, with a small railway carrying the harvest.

The Queens Road starts here and runs along the southern coast of the island, linking Nadi, the Coral Coast and Suva, about two hundred and twenty kilometres in all. It is a mostly good sealed road, with gentle bends, small villages and sudden views of reef and lagoon. Traffic is generally light, but speed limits are low and enforced, and in villages the limit is lower still, with speed bumps and children and dogs on the verge. Vehicles keep to the left, as in Britain.

The weather has two moods: a drier, cooler season from May to October, which is the best time to ride, and a hot, wet season with the possibility of cyclones from November to April. Heavy rain can flood low sections of the road, and fallen branches and potholes are a hazard. Greet people with a smile and a bula, the Fijian welcome, and you will be answered warmly. If you are offered kava, a mildly numbing drink made from a root, it is polite to accept at least one bowl, though it tastes like muddy water.
t.suva@-18.1,178.5:
Suva is the capital of Fiji, and the wettest big town you are likely to ride into. It sits on a hilly peninsula between Laucala Bay and a harbour, with rain-clouds banking up on the mountains behind, and it receives something like three metres of rain a year, so the vegetation is thick and the air smells of warm earth. Suva became the capital in 1882, when the colonial government moved here from Levuka, and the centre still has a scattering of wooden colonial buildings, a grand government house and a long seafront with a view out to the reef. About seventy-seven thousand people live in the city, and the metropolitan area is much larger.

The municipal market is the heart of it, a huge hall of fruit, root crops, kava, fish and spices, sold by women who have been doing it all their lives. The Fiji Museum, in the botanical gardens, holds a fine collection of canoes, war clubs and relics from the cannibal past, and the history it tells is honest and compelling. The university draws students from all over the Pacific, so the cafés on the main streets are full of languages. In the evening, Albert Park, where Charles Kingsford Smith landed the first trans-Pacific flight in 1928, is a good place to watch a game of rugby.

The Queens Road ends here, after a run of two hundred and twenty kilometres from Nadi along the Coral Coast. The final stretch passes Pacific Harbour, a purpose-built resort area that calls itself the adventure capital of Fiji, with rafting and diving, and then runs through rainforest, river crossings and villages, with sea views on the left. The road is mostly good, though heavy rain can cause delays, and speeds are low and enforced. Take care on wet tarmac and on the bridges, and watch for pedestrians and dogs.

In Suva, fuel, repair shops, hotels and restaurants are all available, and the traffic is thick and noisy, with buses that stop without warning. For something local, try a plate of kokoda, raw fish marinated in coconut milk and lime juice, or a lovo, a feast cooked in an earth oven. A short ride out, Colo-i-Suva Forest Park has walking tracks, pools and tropical birds, and a good opportunity to cool off. Pack waterproofs, because showers can come out of a clear sky.
t.saint pierre@-21.3,55.5:
Saint-Pierre is the biggest town on the south coast of Réunion, a French island in the Indian Ocean, and it feels like a proper city rather than a resort: some seventy-six thousand people, wide avenues, a lively seafront, a covered market, schools and traffic jams. It is also where you start the long climb toward the volcano, so the first sensation of the ride is leaving the heat of the coast behind.

Réunion is a volcanic island, young and steep. Its two peaks are the dormant Piton des Neiges, the highest point in the Indian Ocean islands at over three thousand metres, and the very active Piton de la Fournaise in the south-east, one of the most active volcanoes in the world. Much of the island is protected as a national park, and the whole landscape of ridges, cirques and ravines was added to the UNESCO list in 2010. That backdrop matters, because the ride from here goes from palm trees and sugar cane to cloud forest and finally to bare lava over barely fifty kilometres.

The road heads inland through the suburbs of Le Tampon, a big town on the slope above, and then up the Plaine des Cafres, a high farming plateau where it can be ten or fifteen degrees cooler than the shore. Cows graze on green pasture that looks oddly like the Alps, and the air smells of eucalyptus and wet earth. Corners are mostly broad and smooth. You should still expect rain, slippery patches under the trees and sudden mist, as the clouds tend to build against the mountains from mid-morning on.

Before you leave town, do the practical jobs. Saint-Pierre has all the fuel, cash and food you could want, and there is little to buy on the volcano road except a coffee at the plateau villages. The seafront is worth a slow look in the morning, with market stalls selling vanilla, rum infused with fruits and spices, and the local rice-and-meat dishes called rougail and cari, usually spicy and eaten with lentils. Start early: on this island the best light, clearest views and driest roads are all before noon.
t.pas de bellecombe@-21.2,55.7:
The road ends at a railing, and beyond it the ground falls away into a huge crater. Pas de Bellecombe is the viewpoint on the rim of the Enclos Fouqué, the vast caldera wall that contains Piton de la Fournaise, and it sits at around twenty-three hundred metres. Standing here you look down about a hundred metres onto a flat floor of black lava, with the small cinder cone of Formica Leo in the foreground and the main volcanic cone rising beyond it, rust and charcoal and sometimes steaming.

Getting here is a quiet pleasure. From the plateau village of Bourg-Murat, the forest road climbs through tree heather and then through fog-soaked scrub that gets thinner and lower until you are riding across a landscape that looks like another planet. The road is narrow and mostly smooth, with long bends, and the temperature falls fast. Wind can be harsh, clouds often roll in by early afternoon, and visibility can drop to a few metres, so the cleanest views come before ten in the morning. Bring a warm layer; it can feel like autumn in the middle of the tropics.

The volcano is one of the most active on Earth and erupts several times in a typical year, usually from vents inside the enclosure, which is why the area is monitored closely. When an eruption is under way or the alert level is raised, the prefecture can close the road, the car park and the trails, so check the local news before committing. Most eruptions are effusive, with lava flowing slowly across the old floor, rather than violent explosions, but the authorities do not take chances.

A staircase leads down from the viewpoint for those who want to walk the crater. It is a serious hike, across rough lava, and the weather can change quickly. On a motorbike, I would simply enjoy the view, drink something warm from the supplies you brought, and watch the clouds shift across the cone.
t.forgotten world highway point 1@-38.9,17:
Taumarunui is where the Forgotten World Highway starts, and the name of the road is not a marketing slogan so much as a fair description. The town stands where the Ongarue and Whanganui rivers meet, in the heart of the North Island, and it was once a bustling railway and river port, with paddle steamers carrying passengers and goods down the Whanganui toward the coast. The railway still passes through, but the trains are fewer, and the town has the quiet, slightly faded look of a place that has seen busier days.

The Whanganui River, which flows past, is sacred to the local Maori, who consider it an ancestor, and in 2017 it was granted legal personhood, the first river in the world to be so recognised. Canoeists and kayakers paddle the upper river, and the Whanganui River Road, a winding backroad, follows part of it. The land around is rugged, steep and forested, with sheep and cattle farms on the cleared hills.

For riders, Taumarunui is the last proper stop before a long, remote road. State Highway 43, the Forgotten World Highway, runs about a hundred and fifty kilometres across the hill country to Stratford, through some of the emptiest and most remarkable scenery in the North Island. It has tight bends, steep hills, one-lane bridges, a tunnel and a section of unsealed road, so it is slow, and the distance takes longer than the map suggests. Start early, and allow a full day.

Fuel is the main concern. Carry water and snacks, and buy lunch here, or plan to eat at the pub in Whangamomona, which is open for meals. Mobile coverage is patchy along the highway, so tell someone your plan.

The weather can vary, with sunshine in the morning and fog or rain by afternoon, and winters are cold and wet, with ice on the higher sections. A good waterproof and warm gloves are worth packing. A coffee at one of the local cafes before you leave, a quick check of the bike and a good look at the sky is the right way to begin.
